stories.title: Cuba: Ten Years after the Death of Fidel Castro
stories.summary: The country is in a perilous state, but it's not simply the result of U.S. imperialism. The post Cuba: Ten Years after the Death of Fidel Castro appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Cuba without electricity (Shutterstock)

Originally published in MicroMega .

The Cuban government will commemorate the tenth anniversary of Fidel Castro’s death amid the worst economic crisis since the victory of the revolution in 1959. This was the immediate outcome of the U.S. military intervention and kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro on January 3 of this year. The U.S. victory resulted in an immediate cutoff of Venezuelan oil shipments that together with the marked deterioration of the electrical plants, considerably aggravated the already existing bad economic situation on the island. At this point, blackouts spread over the whole country with its very damaging effects on transport, economic activity, and Cuban homes.

In a triumphalist mood after the Venezuelan intervention, Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio proceeded to develop a similar plan for Cuba, with the expectation that an economic strangulation of the island, going way beyond the measures associated with the economic blockade adopted in the early 1960s, would cause extreme economic hardships. This would lead some Cuban leaders to emulate the Venezuelan bureaucrats led by Delcy Rodriguez to toe the U.S. line, thereby obviating the need for a military occupation of the country. The new Trump/Rubio policies further reduced tourism to Cuba and forced out predominantly Spanish companies such as Meliá (with over 30 hotels on the island), thus leaving the door open for a future takeover by U.S. hotel giants. The Canadian Sherritt Corporation, in charge of the extraction of Cuban cobalt and nickel, was compelled to sign an agreement to sell most of its shares to Gillon Capital LLC, a firm led by Ray Washburn, a former official in the first Trump administration.

These drastic U.S. measures are part of what Rafael Rojas, a Cuban liberal democratic writer residing in Mexico, called “the road towards a recolonization of Cuba.”

The Cuban Government’s Response

In a desperate effort to ensure its economic survival while retaining economic and political control, Cuban Prime Minister Manuel Marrero Cruz announced on June 18 a 176-point program to restructure the Cuban economy, arguing that “socialist planning does not exclude but most incorporate and regulate the rules of the market.” These measures tending toward capitalism included major changes such as:

Selling stock to Cuban and foreign investors in state enterprises and reducing the Cuban state monopoly of foreign trade;

Inviting private enterprises to invest in land owned by the Cuban government that will be granted to them in usufruct, i.e., it can be cultivated for profit but not bought or sold.

Elimination of price controls as well as the universal subsidies of basic products through the tarjeta (ration card) to be replaced by income-tested programs for the most vulnerable people.

PYMES (small and medium-sized private enterprises) will no longer be limited to hiring up to 100 workers. Henceforward, businesses that surpass this limit will be called “private enterprises.”

Salary levels negotiated by the workers and the state-controlled unions (that have no right to strike) must depend on the economic and financial capacity of the individual enterprises, making national or industry-wide salary levels irrelevant.

As this 176-point program is gradually being implemented, there is also a parallel process of informal privatization through the PYMES—fueled by remittances from abroad that benefit about half the population although Black Cubans are greatly underrepresented—as in the opening of new retail outlets selling imported goods. Potentially more important is the Trump administration allowing the sale of oil to the Cuban private sector, gasoline that can now be obtained at elevated prices at private gas stations.

Cuban Realities before the U.S. coup in Venezuela

Poverty and inequality had already greatly increased, although the Cuban government stopped the publication of relevant data more than two decades ago. In this context of scarcity and blackouts, street protests have marked the Cuban political scene, especially after the nationwide protests that broke out on July 11, 2021. Numerous local protests have followed since then. Strong repressive measures have been taken against these protestors. Although few injuries and no deaths have been registered because of these events, property damage has taken place in several places that have been, in many cases, punished with 20-year prison sentences. Human rights organizations have estimated that there are more than 1,000 political prisoners in Cuba.

The pervasive sense of powerlessness and hopelessness faced by the Cuban people has powerfully contributed to a massive emigration since the early 2020s. According to the official National Office of Statistics and Information (ONEI) Cuba had a population of over 11 million people on December 31, 2021, while the same office stipulated that at the beginning of 2026, Cuba’s population had declined to about 9.4 million people. However, independent demographer Juan Carlos Albizu-Campos estimates that the Cuban population in 2026 was 8-8.62 million. Since the composition of the emigration has tended to concentrate on younger people, this has also considerably worsened the dependency of a growing older generation on the economic productivity of economically active younger cohorts.

The dramatic situation confronted by the Cuban people has also contributed to a very disturbing phenomenon; namely, the growth of pro-U.S. sentiments among many Cubans. Deplorably, the bulk of the Cuban opposition, including its liberal democratic section, has accommodated itself to this political development, instead of unambiguously criticizing it based on the premise that the problems of the Cuban people are for the Cubans themselves to resolve without the intervention of the United States, the principal imperial power today.

What is To Blame? A False Dilemma

The Cuban government and its supporters abroad attribute all Cuban economic problems to U.S. imperialism. The Cuban right-wing opposition especially in south Florida at best ignores the effects of the U.S. blockade and generally welcomes Washington’s attribution of Cuba’s economic problems solely to the Communist system.

The U.S. blockade adopted in the early 1960s has had substantial negative effects on the Cuban economy. It not only forbids U.S. investment and direct trade with the island—with some often-complicated exceptions adopted during the last three decades—but has also penalized banks, enterprises, and ships of third countries that maintain economic ties with the island. In the past, the aid provided by the USSR and later by Venezuela as well as trade relations with Canada and the European Union have compensated to a significant extent the losses caused by the U.S. blockade. However, Trump’s policy of economic strangulation during 2026 has had an overwhelming effect and has become by far the principal factor negatively affecting the Cuban economy.

Over the long haul however, the endogenous factors affecting Cuban economic performance have been more significant in accounting for the problems of the Cuban economy. Since 1959, the Cuban economy has been highly centralized and bureaucratic, lacking transparency and open public discussion of most of its fundamental problems. Authentic feedback, accurate information, and independent initiatives from below are discouraged by its bureaucratic organization. The lack of worker control from below and inadequate material and political incentives, such as would exist in an authentic democracy, substantially create apathy, and thus inefficiency. In Politics and Markets, the political scientist Charles E. Lindblom argued that Soviet-type societies tend to have strong thumbs, but no fingers. Strong thumbs allow the government to mobilize large numbers of people to carry out homogeneous, routinized, and repetitive tasks—as in a national vaccination campaign—while the lack of fingers is a disaster when it comes to housing, personal services, and retail establishments where distinctions are crucial considerations, for example concerning the quantity and variety of food or housing, let alone the size, color, and style of merchandise.

Lack of attention to expert feedback has often been a key factor in bringing about disastrous Cuban government policies. On January 1, 2021 in the midst of the COVID epidemic, for instance, the government carried out the long delayed monetary reform, when a newly and strongly overvalued peso unleashed a huge inflationary wave, exactly as predicted by independent Cuban economists such as Carmelo Mesa-Lago. The government sought to retain centralized control from the top at any price. During the ineffective agrarian reforms, the government of Raul Castro implemented a stingy land distribution program while leaving Acopio , the agency in charge of appropriating most of the small farmers produce at prices unilaterally established by the government, in unchallenged control. No wonder that Cuba Is forced to import 80 percent of the food consumed by its people.

Fidel Castro’s Politics from Above

In the 1950s, a young Fidel Castro, unrestrained by firm ideological commitments, followed a consistent policy of armed struggle against Batista’s military dictatorship based on the well-founded assumption that the dictatorship would not voluntarily give up power. But at the same time, his Twenty-sixth of July movement remained under his personal political control. As he put it in a 1954 letter to his then friend Luis Conte Aguero: “The [movement’s] apparatus of propaganda and organization must be such and so powerful that it will implacably destroy him who will create tendencies, cliques, or schisms of will rise against the movement.”

Once in power in 1959 and buoyed by overwhelming popular support, Fidel introduced many radical but non-Communist laws such as urban housing and agrarian reform that May. However, as U.S. opposition notably increased after the agrarian reform—and under the political pressure of the movement’s pro-Communist wing led by this brother Raúl (a former member of the old pro-Moscow Communist party’s youth wing) and by independent Communist Ernesto “Che” Guevara—Fidel threw his lot in with a Soviet alliance. Like the leaders of other countries such as India, Indonesia, and Egypt, he was to obtain arms and economic aid from the Soviet bloc. But going well beyond that aid, it also involved installing a Soviet-type system on the island.

There was an “elective affinity” between Fidel Castro’s views on how to control from above his movement and the Soviet model, only adding to that model the notion of popular participation in huge demonstrations supporting what the government had already decided, but without control or decision-making from below. It is significant that in implementing the agrarian reform the Cuban government would promptly respond to peasant grievances by bringing in the Rebel Army and taking over and later nationalizing those properties but without empowering the campesinos themselves.

This personal and often arbitrary control from above would become a key element of numerous economic problems. For example, Castro conducted an economically disastrous campaign for a ten-million-ton sugar crop in 1970, which failed to achieve its goals and greatly disrupted the rest of the economy. His penchant for economic “gigantism” led him to carry out such projects as the unnecessary and wasteful eight-lane highway traversing a good part of Cuba.

Finally, Cuba deserves a better choice than that between an undemocratic and economically damaging version of the Soviet system and the reestablishment of a U.S. colonialism that will neither be democratic nor materially benefit most people.

This article was originally published on November 2?, 2026 in MicroMega, a prominent left-wing political and intellectual journal in Italy.

stories.title: The Next Congress Should Scrutinize the U.S.-Nigeria Security Partnership
stories.summary: Military operations can disrupt armed groups, but they can’t deliver lasting security unless respect for human rights is guaranteed. The post The Next Congress Should Scrutinize the U.S.-Nigeria Security Partnership appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A police officer in Lagos, Nigeria (Shutterstock)

This fall in Washington, I met with congressional staff, State Department officials, and other Nigeria observers to discuss a country facing one of the world’s most complex security crises.

After years of documenting violence across Nigeria, I have become convinced that military action alone cannot resolve the crisis. As Abuja and Washington deepen their security partnership, the challenge is not simply to defeat armed groups and other violent actors, but to build a response that delivers both security and justice.

The Danger of Abusive Operations

Nigeria faces a range of serious security challenges. The Islamist insurgency group Boko Haram and its splinter faction, the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), continue to attack communities in the northeast. Bandit gangs that emerged following years of farmer-herder violence in the northwest carry out killings, kidnap people for ransom, and terrorize communities. Violence persists in the Middle Belt, driven by a complex mix of Islamist insurgency, intercommunal tensions, and banditry.

At the same time, Nigerian security forces continue to respond to these threats through military operations that have themselves raised serious human rights concerns.

The United States, a long-standing security partner of Nigeria, has in recent years expanded intelligence sharing, training, and security cooperation with Nigerian authorities. Earlier this year, a joint U.S.-Nigeria operation reportedly killed Abu-Bilal al-Minuki, a senior ISIS leader and a key figure in the group’s global operations , underscoring the growing depth of the partnership.

Much of Washington’s recent focus on Nigeria has been driven by concerns about violence affecting Christian communities . These concerns continue to shape engagement and have elevated Nigeria on the U.S. policy agenda. My recent discussions in Washington, however, suggest a growing appreciation, both on the Hill and among State Department officials, of the complexity of Nigeria’s security issues and the need for solutions that move beyond a single narrative to address the diverse drivers of violence across the country.

That shift is important because Nigeria’s insecurity cannot be reduced to a simple Christian-versus-Muslim conflict, in a country that is close to half and half. Both Christians and Muslims have suffered from violence across northern Nigeria. While religion and identity are important dimensions of some conflicts, particularly in the culturally diverse Middle Belt, they cannot fully explain the diverse drivers of insecurity across the country . A more nuanced understanding is essential to developing effective responses.

The question for the United States, therefore, is not simply how to support Nigeria’s military response, but how to ensure that its assistance strengthens the protection of ordinary people and communities affected by a lack of accountability and the rule of law as well as by insecurity.

These are not peripheral issues.

When military operations harm the very people they are meant to protect — and those responsible are not held accountable — communities can lose confidence in security institutions and government authorities. Abusive operations can deepen grievances, create openings for recruitment by armed groups, and undermine cooperation with authorities, making it harder to reduce violence and protect communities over the long term.

U.S. assistance should not focus narrowly on supporting Nigeria’s capacity to respond to armed groups and other violent actors. U.S. efforts should also focus on measures that strengthen accountability, improve protection of communities, and build public trust in security institutions. These elements are essential to a security response capable of addressing immediate threats while laying the foundation for lasting peace and stability.

Accountability for Victims of Airstrikes

One area where this matters is Nigeria’s growing reliance on air power. Airstrikes and unmanned aerial vehicles have become a central feature of military operations against insurgents and bandit gangs. Recognizing the risks posed to civilians and communities caught in the violence, U.S. support has helped encourage efforts by the Nigerian Air Force to develop a Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response framework. This is an important step in the right direction.

Yet recent incidents underscore why such efforts must move beyond policy commitments and produce measurable results.

Last spring, a Nigerian military airstrike in the northeast targeting what authorities described as a Boko Haram or ISWAP logistics hub struck a market . Local sources reported up to 200 deaths , and the federal government acknowledged that there were some civilian casualties.

Less than a month later, another airstrike targeting bandits in a market in northwest Nigeria reportedly killed more than 100 people, though the military disputed this.

These incidents are not isolated. Since 2017, Nigerian military airstrikes have reportedly killed hundreds of ordinary people . Yet investigations have rarely resulted in public findings, meaningful accountability, or adequate remedies for victims and affected communities. The result is a growing accountability deficit that undermines public trust and raises serious concerns about human rights protection and safeguarding human life.

For civilian harm mitigation to be more than a paper exercise, Nigerian authorities should ensure prompt, transparent investigations into alleged abuses and provide victims with effective remedies. These safeguards should be embedded across all security services involved in operations to address insecurity.

Trials Without Justice

Another crucial accountability gap is visible in Nigeria’s justice sector. Nigeria has sought to demonstrate progress through mass terrorism trials involving hundreds of Boko Haram suspects. The U.S. has welcomed these efforts, with U.S. officials praising the convictions of 386 defendants during the latest phase of the proceedings .

Yet the effectiveness of a justice system cannot be measured solely by the number of convictions it produces. It should be judged by whether prosecutions are evidence-based, fair, and focused on those most responsible for serious crimes. In fact, such mass trials hardly seem capable of providing justice, which should be based on individual criminal actions.

My recent observations of Boko Haram-related terrorism trials suggest that Nigeria remains far from that goal. While accountability for that group’s widespread abuses is urgently needed, the proceedings largely targeted low-level suspects accused of providing material support to armed groups. In some cases, people who were prosecuted apparently were forced against their will to provide food, shelter, or other benefits to insurgent fighters — while those most responsible for grave abuses often remained beyond the reach of justice.

In many of the cases observed, convictions relied heavily on guilty pleas that may have been coerced with the threat of disproportionate punishments, with no witness testimony or other evidence tested through adversarial proceedings. These concerns raise important questions about both due process and the credibility of outcomes.

The result is a familiar pattern. In the case of airstrikes, communities are left without answers about what happened, who was responsible, and what remedies they are entitled to. In the terrorism trials, convictions are secured, but the proceedings are not delivering real justice for the most serious crimes.

Rethinking Security

The lesson from Nigeria’s security crisis is clear. Military operations can disrupt armed groups and other violent actors, but they cannot deliver lasting security unless respect for human rights is guaranteed. As the United States deepens its engagement with Nigeria, it should support efforts that place accountability, civilian protection, and the rule of law at the center of the response to insecurity.

Congress can play an important role by considering human rights conditions to security assistance, holding hearings into allegations of abuses by Nigerian security forces, and pressing the administration to enforce existing safeguards, including the Leahy Laws. With a change in congressional leadership in January 2027, lawmakers will have an opportunity to scrutinize U.S. security cooperation with Nigeria and push for greater accountability.

Ultimately, the measure of success will not be how many operations are conducted, but by whether Nigerians are safer, access to justice has improved, and public trust in state institutions has been strengthened. This requires respect for human rights, accountability for abuses, and security responses that do not deepen the very grievances they seek to address.

stories.title: War Reveals a Global Food System Tethered to Fossil Fuels
stories.summary: The Iran war has shuttered refineries in the Persian Gulf and throttled the production of sulfur, which is critical for making fertilizer needed to feed the world. The crisis, expected to raise grocery prices, hints at an unintended consequence of the fossil fuel phaseout. Read more on E360 →
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A pile of sulfur at an oil refinery in Cartagena, Spain. Sulfur, a byproduct of refining, is needed to make phosphate fertilizer. Angel Garcia / Bloomberg via Getty Images

ANALYSIS

The Iran war has shuttered refineries in the Persian Gulf and throttled the production of sulfur, which is critical for making fertilizer needed to feed the world. The crisis, expected to raise grocery prices, hints at an unintended consequence of the fossil fuel phaseout.

By Fred Pearce • November 24, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

Millions of farmers around the world are living in fear that their crop yields will falter in the coming months. They blame the Iran war, which has reduced supplies of the phosphate fertilizer vital for a successful harvest by 40 percent and raised its price beyond the reach of many.

But few farmers will likely know that their reliance on Persian Gulf states for much of their phosphate fertilizer is an outgrowth of a global effort more than 30 years ago to banish a major environmental scourge — the sulfur emissions from power plants that caused acid rain.

Those efforts required oil and natural gas refineries in the Gulf and elsewhere to strip sulfur from their products. That waste sulfur swiftly became the go-to feedstock for making sulfuric acid, the world’s most widely used industrial chemical, and one that is essential when processing phosphate rock to make phosphate fertilizer. Sulfur prices tumbled and, unable to compete, almost all the world’s sulfur mines shut. Soon, nearly half of internationally traded sulfur was being supplied by refineries in the Gulf. Or it was until those supplies were cut off in 2026.

Today, more than 95 percent of the world’s sulfur comes from oil and natural gas refineries.

There isn’t yet any reliable data on crop yields following the fertilizer drought: Most crops are still in the ground. But farmers from Brazil to India to southern Africa await with trepidation the impact on their upcoming harvests.

The rest of the world should be equally concerned. Analysts expect the crisis will cut crop yields in 2027 and beyond, raising food prices everywhere for years to come. The World Food Programme warns that, in combination with El Niño , the shortage could bring hunger to at least an additional 49 million people.

Meanwhile, analysts warn that the potential impact of the sulfur crisis on fertilizer production is likely to be just a foretaste of what will happen as the world phases out fossil fuels. An end to refining oil and natural gas would also halt the supply of waste sulfur at a time when demand is set to increase due to greater need for fertilizer and for refining metal ores for the fast-growing batteries market, says Mark Maslin, a geographer at University College London who has tracked the trade.

“My concern is that green tech outbids the fertilizer industry for the limited, more expensive sulfur supply,” he says, “creating an issue with food production, particularly in developing countries.”

A farmer spreads fertilizer on his land in Indian Kashmir. Firdous Nazir / NurPhoto via AP

Using waste sulfur from refineries to make sulfuric acid should be a textbook example of how circular economies work, with one industry’s discards becoming the feedstock for another. Tens of millions of tons of waste sulfur from refineries is used in the manufacture of everything from rubber tires to paper. Before the war, the fertilizer industry absorbed more than half of the world’s available sulfuric acid to extract phosphorus from rocks and make a product that helps to feed the world. Sulfuric acid is also used to extract copper, nickel, and cobalt from ores to make the batteries that run electric vehicles — a critical part of international efforts to reach net-zero carbon emissions by midcentury.

And yet that green virtue in 2026 turned into a liability. During the Iran conflict, damaged production plants and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the main shipping route from Gulf refineries to sulfur markets, cut off 45 percent of the world’s trade in this strategically vital waste product. (While Gulf producers have been able to export some oil and natural gas through pipelines to the Red Sea, there are no pipelines that can handle dry, solid sulfur.)

This sudden sulfur shortfall has caught governments and producers without a Plan B, says MacDonald Amoah, an analyst of critical minerals for the Payne Institute for Public Policy at the Colorado School of Mines. Because sulfur has been regarded as a waste product, it has been little monitored by trade bodies. As it happens, this industrial material, essential for feeding the world, has no strategic reserves.

Many fertilizer producers have shut down because their ultimate customers, farmers, can no longer pay for the product.

In the 1980s, acid rain was a headline-grabbing environmental scourge. Emissions of sulfur dioxide from power stations burning sulfur-rich fossil fuels turned the rain across Europe and much of North America as acidic as lemon juice. Forests from the Appalachian Mountains to the Carpathians in Eastern Europe lost foliage and died; acid-drenched soils released toxic metals, killing fish in rivers and lakes.

The scourge was high politics, too. Canada’s environment minister complained to a visiting Ronald Reagan that his nation’s damaged forests and lakes were at the end of a “gigantic exhaust pipe” that began in the eastern United States. Swedish and Norwegian governments blamed British power stations for their hundreds of fishless lakes.

Governments eventually acted, requiring the scrubbing of sulfur dioxide from power station flue gases. Power companies in turn demanded that refiners supplying oil and natural gas remove the sulfur at source. The result of this international clean-up was a vast new waste stream of elemental sulfur that soon found a market as a feedstock for manufacturing sulfuric acid.

By century’s end, the world was awash with cheap waste sulfur. The market price had fallen by 80 percent, forcing mines from Sicily and Mexico to the salt domes of Texas out of business. Today, more than 95 percent of the world’s sulfur comes from oil and natural gas refineries, and almost half of international trade is through the Strait of Hormuz.

Cargo ships anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Bandar Abbas, Iran. Amirhosein Khorgooi / AP Photo

Most discussion about the resource implications of the Iran war has concentrated on disruption to the Gulf’s oil and natural gas exports. But the war has also hindered the production of the two most critical fertilizers in the world: nitrogen-based ammonia, which is made in the Gulf using hydrogen extracted from natural gas, and phosphate fertilizer, whose manufacture requires sulfur extracted from hydrocarbon refining. The conflict has cut the amount of nitrogen supplied to farmers by about a quarter but phosphate supplies by 40 percent.

As the war has progressed, the supply of sulfur has continued to shrink. In May, China, the world’s largest exporter of sulfuric acid, banned sales to foreign manufacturers to protect its own fertilizer supplies. Then in August, Ukrainian drones struck Gazprom’s Astrakhan gas processing plant, knocking out 60 percent of Russia’s sulfur production.

With supplies cut and prices up by more than a third, sometimes exceeding $1,000 per metric ton, much of the sulfur that has been available has been snapped up by the mining industry, which can afford the higher prices. The price hike has left phosphate fertilizer producers in a bind. Many have shut down because their ultimate customers, farmers, cannot pay for the product. Mosaic, one of the world’s biggest manufacturers, more than halved its U.S. production in 2026 and has announced plans to shut one plant for six months starting in December. “Without affordable sulfur,” production superintendent Hector Mier said last month, the company was “forced to curtail production. That means less fertilizer for farmers and less food grown in American farmland.” Saudi and Brazilian plants have also closed.

As less fertilizer is added to soils, says an analyst, there will be an “erosion of agricultural productivity in many countries.”

Brendan Rice, an agribusiness analyst for the Washington, D.C.-based International Food Policy Research Institute, warns that as less phosphate fertilizer is added to soils, there will be “a slow-rolling erosion of agricultural productivity in many countries” stretching through 2027 and beyond.

The first clear signs of the downturn may emerge in the next three months with the harvest of rice in India and Thailand, soy in Brazil, and corn in southern Africa. Amoah says it will “lock in grocery inflation for years.”

What will happen if the Gulf conflict continues to restrict sulfur supplies?

There is no immediate prospect of a revival of sulfur mining. Only two mines remain open: the Osiek Mine in southern Poland and the Kawah Ijen volcano on the Indonesian island of Java, where a few hundred intrepid miners armed with hand tools clamber down into the crater to dig out yellow blocks of elemental sulfur, which they haul to the surface in bamboo baskets. Neither mine could quickly increase production, analysts say. And a widespread reopening of closed mines would be a costly and risky enterprise when Gulf production of cheap sulfur could resume at least as quickly.

A miner gathers sulfur from Kawah Ijen, an active volcano on the Indonesian island of Java. Oscar Espinosa / SOPA Images / LightRocket via Getty Images

There is sulfur stockpiled at a few refineries — notably some 10 million metric tons around tar-sands deposits in the Canadian province of Alberta, some of which is sent to fertilizer manufacturers in Canada and the U.S. But scaling up distribution quickly for the international market would be challenging. “Every tonne must be excavated off the block, trucked to a melting site, melted, formed, and railed to Vancouver for vessel loading,” says Fiona Boyd , a director of London-based Acuity Commodities. “[It’s] a lengthy and expensive process.”

Experts predict that Gulf supplies of sulfur will eventually resume. But that will only postpone the day, says Maslin, when the world faces a long-term sulfur crunch as demand rises while supplies falter.

On the demand side, most observers expect a rapid increase in the use of sulfuric acid as more metals are refined to make batteries. And as the world’s population continues to rise, feeding more people will also likely require more sulfur to make more phosphorus fertilizer. Overall, Maslin sees the market growing by around 60 percent to 400 million metric tons by midcentury.

Farmers could reduce their use of synthetic fertilizers by nourishing their soils with animal manure and farm waste.

But at the same time, he says, supply is set to crash as the world’s energy system decarbonizes, with consumption peaking and then falling sharply over the next three decades, slashing the production of sulfur waste at refineries. In 2022, Maslin and his University College London colleagues calculated that shifting away from fossil fuels “could create a shortfall of sulfuric acid as large as 320 million [metric tons], or 130 percent of present-day production.”

The supply crunch would drive up the cost of sulfur, Maslin said. Then, as now, farmers — and the world’s food supply — would be the likely losers.

To address the shortfall, farmers could reduce their dependence on both nitrogen and phosphate fertilizers by nourishing their soils organically. Animal manure and organic farm wastes are rich in both chemicals. But few agriculturalists expect such methods to do more than moderate rising demand for synthetic fertilizer — and the sulfur needed to make it.

So where will the sulfur come from? We could go back to large-scale mining. Unlike some strategic materials, the world is not short of geological sulfur. It is the 13th most abundant element in the Earth’s crust, found in volcanoes, salt domes, and in sedimentary deposits created by the evaporation of seawater.

A tractor spreads fertilizer on a soybean field in Goias, Brazil. Mateus Bonomi / Anadolu Agency via Getty Images

But Maslin warns of the risks. “Direct mining of elemental sulfur is dirty, toxic, [and] destructive.” To minimize the damage, he says, “the world needs to cut demand by recycling and using alternative industrial technologies that avoid intensive use of sulfuric acid.” Widespread commercial recycling of sulfur has potential. Sulfuric acid is a major component of widely used lead-acid batteries, for instance. In the U.S. it is widely recycled along with lead.

Another approach is to cut demand for sulfur’s biggest use — making phosphate fertilizer — by recycling the phosphates found in human sewage, which is where much of the material used to grow our food ends up.

More than half the world’s population is now connected to sewage systems. Sewage sludge from treatment works may contain industrial contaminants but is generally considered safe for application to cropland and often sold or given to farmers in developed countries, notably the U.K. and the U.S. Sludge incinerators in Japan and Germany sell their leftover ash, still rich in phosphates, either to farmers or to fertilizer manufacturers. Willem Schipper, a Dutch consultant in industrial chemistry, calculates that current sewage systems worldwide could deliver around a million metric tons of phosphates each year. That is roughly 3 percent of what is mined each year, but it would trim the need for both sulfur and phosphate, a rock that is itself in increasingly short supply.

By removing phosphates from raw sewage at treatment works, recycling would also reduce the environmental impacts of high levels of phosphates in rivers, where the chemical spurs the growth of plants and algae that block sunlight from penetrating the water and lower oxygen levels. So, while one version of a circular economy might falter as fossil fuels are sidelined, another, smaller circular economy could emerge.

stories.body:
A world made safe for spheres of influence.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

Pundits who dismissed the Shenzhen summit as a mere photo-op lacking substance missed the point. The significance of the conclave was precisely its enframing symbolism, showcasing a new world in which the rules-based order has been supplanted by spheres of influence accommodating each other.

The city of Shenzhen itself is a prism through which we can observe today’s power relations and the evolution of events over recent decades bringing us to this point.

Unplugged Computers in China’s Future Tech Hub

I first visited Shenzhen in 1986, arriving there by tram from Hong Kong and walking across the mainland border. There was barely any bustle, no crowds or traffic and a couple of tall buildings at the most. At our modest hotel, a squatting gardener was clipping the grass with a pair of scissors. The place still exuded the languorous vibe of the fishing village of 30,000 it had been not long before it was designated a “special economic zone” by Deng Xiaoping to attract foreign capital and technology.

On an inspection tour of sprouting industrial parks with then-former California governor Jerry Brown, our hosts proudly showed us what they called a tech hub. What then passed for “data centers” were cavernous, virtually empty warehouses with scores of desktop computers on worktables gathering dust — none were even plugged in.

What seemed embarrassing at the time turned out to be beyond impressive 40 years later. Shenzhen today is a literally glittering technopolis of 20 million people regarded as China’s “Silicon Valley” where Huawei, Tencent, DJI and BYD are all located. It is the center of gravity of China’s AI battle with the United States.

The invitation to visit had come some years earlier from Xi Zhongxun, then Party chief of Guangdong province (where Shenzhen is located) and the father of China’s current leader, Xi Jinping. The elder Xi had come to California in 1980 looking for investment in the special economic zone as a key platform of Deng’s policy of “reform and opening up” to the world. On that visit, he met Gov. Jerry Brown and toured the state, including stops at tech sites in the then-fledgling Silicon Valley (Apple and Intel were about it in those days) and Disneyland, where he gamely shook hands with Mickey Mouse.

Years later in 2012, when Brown was governor again for a second time, Xi Jinping, then-vice-president of China on his way to the top, visited California. The irony was not lost on either leader when the governor inquired whether China was interested in helping finance California’s bullet train, already in the works for nearly 20 years.

A Chinese delegation later met with the governor at the Peninsula Hotel in Beverly Hills to discuss possibilities, but the idea never panned out. Those who had once come cup in hand to the Golden State now offered financing terms too tough to abide. By 2026, China had built a 30,000-mile network of bullet trains spanning its vast country. California and the U.S. still have yet to build one.

On that 1986 trip to China, Brown and I also met at Zhongnanhai, the secluded leader’s compound in Beijing, with the ideology chief and youngest member of the ruling Communist Party Politburo at the time, Hu Qili. In a wide-ranging conversation that touched on topics from the “spiritual pollution” of Western influence to Tibetan Buddhism, Hu noted that the Chinese military had reduced its forces by one million soldiers. Many military installations, he said, were converting to commercial applications in light industry and heavy-truck production. Several military aircraft plants were now making refrigerators and motorcycles.

To this, Brown quipped, “If the army is making refrigerators, you must think the polar bear [what the Chinese called Russia] is hibernating.” Laughing, Hu simply replied that since Russia “couldn’t even consolidate control of Cambodia, it is only inviting great trouble to try anything with China.”

Opening then to America while hostile to an ebbing Soviet empire, Hu insisted that “China’s armed forces are sufficient to resist hegemonist efforts from the bear if they come.”

By the time I saw Hu again in 1988, Mikhail Gorbachev had come to power in the Kremlin, attracting some sympathy among reformers in China and inspiring a growing youth movement with his ideas of perestroika and glasnost. Enough of a thaw was in the works that Hu asked me to convey “fraternal greetings” to Aleksandr Yakovlev, then the Soviet party’s main reformist thinker, on my next stop in Moscow. Read Noema in print.

“The one key power left out of the 1945 Yalta talks that shaped the international order in the dying days of World War II is now setting the agenda for what comes next.”

The Tiananmen Turn

It was in that atmosphere that Gorbachev visited Beijing in May 1989 and met with Premier Zhao Ziyang as tensions with the authorities were mounting on Tiananmen Square. In the wake of the student massacre that June, the liberal-leaning Zhao was purged for revealing “state secrets” to Gorbachev by telling him that Deng, who would order the repression, remained the power behind the throne even though he had formally retired. Hu was also purged.

This was a “ludicrous accusation,” Gorbachev told me later. The real issue, as he saw it, was his advice that the student occupation should be defused politically through negotiation, not force. “I was confident a political solution could be found. I was wrong, unfortunately,” the last Soviet leader lamented.

Deng had drawn the line on Party control that Gorbachev was erasing in Moscow. Deng’s open palm on the economy clenched into an iron fist on political reform. Ever since, Gorbachev’s “new thinking” has been vilified in Beijing as a recipe for the collapse of the Party-state, and something to be avoided at all costs.

A World Safe For Spheres Of Influence

When Vladimir Putin emerged in the tumultuous years after the Soviet collapse, China’s sympathy with a more amenable Russia returned. As the post-Cold War years wore on, the “hegemonist threat” for China shifted to America, even as it prospered from the relationship.

In the end, China’s leaders came to strategically favor a trusted autocrat ruthlessly obsessed with dominating his own neighborhood over a meddling America endlessly endeavoring, in their minds, to subvert China’s governing system and keep the nation down. Party ideologues, Xi above all, are convinced that the American political class, implicitly if not explicitly, concurs with Bill Clinton’s remark when he was president that China was on “the wrong side of history.” Like many others in those days, Clinton wrongly presumed trade winds would blow open the society.

With a militarily mighty but economically feeble and dependent Russia at its side, China’s leaders have grown more confident in their capacity to contain America in a world made safe for spheres of influence.

The few words spoken for public consumption at the Shenzhen summit about zones of “civilizational values” and the primacy of state sovereignty over international law were code for the long-standing views of Xi and Putin, which the American president has now openly embraced.

Tech Trips The Thucydides Trap

At the first meeting of the Berggruen Institute’s 21st Century Council with Xi Jinping in 2013, the Party leader boasted that “we have never been closer to realizing the dream of Chinese rejuvenation” after the long climb back from colonial humiliation — invoking that history as if it were yesterday.

As Xi sees it, far from being on the wrong side of history, only the firm hand of the Communist Party could have brought the Middle Kingdom to where it is today and can take it where it must go tomorrow.

In 2015, then Premier Li Keqiang launched a “Made in China 2025” campaign with the goal of conquering the latest technologies from electric vehicles and batteries to artificial intelligence within a decade. Xi sees this conquest as rocket fuel for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, which he is determined to ensure does not fall behind the West and invite domination by outside forces, as it did during the Ming and Qing dynasties of the late 19th Century.

Strategists in Washington across the partisan landscape see China’s unrelenting resolve to reach its goals as an existential threat to America’s technological supremacy, and all that implies in terms of military might and geopolitical sway.

At our 2013 meeting, Xi pointedly raised an historical reference to “the Thucydides Trap,” whereby a rising power inevitably runs into conflict with an established power, only to say China would seek to avoid it. By now, though, it is clear that of all the contested issues between the U.S. and China, technology is most likely to trip the trap. The Nvidia episode is but one skirmish in a larger battle.

Shenzhen Supplants Yalta

If I were to have a conversation with the ideology chief on the Politburo today, as I had with Hu decades ago, here is what I would imagine him saying: “We have demonstrated we can go head-to-head with America on AI and technology. Today our military is reinvigorated. We have the largest navy in the world and are scaling up our nuclear arsenal toward parity with the U.S. and Russia. To be sure, America remains a formidable foe with the legacy of hegemonist ambitions. But let’s be serious. It is crumbling within. Its aging systems are plagued by outages. It can’t even build one bullet train.”

For Xi, hosting both leaders of the other great powers in Shenzhen, where China’s tech prowess is on full display, is the ultimate icing on the cake of rejuvenation. The one key power left out of the 1945 Yalta talks that shaped the international order in the dying days of World War II is now setting the agenda for what comes next.

stories.body:
Regulation alone won’t fix the conditions that have earned China the reputation of the “Wild East.”

Jane Qiu is an independent science writer in Beijing.

BEIJING — In March 2023, four-year-old Mei in Shanghai was diagnosed with a rare genetic mutation linked to developmental delay and autism-like traits. Although her condition was mild and she improved with therapy and special education, her parents remained worried about her future. Hopeful for a cure, they paid Qiu Zilong, a renowned neuroscientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and his team $860,000 to develop a customized gene therapy. The treatment, which used adeno-associated viruses to deliver gene editors to the brain, had been approved by Xinhua Hospital, a leading hospital for rare diseases.

On March 24, 2025, trillions of viral particles carrying gene editors were injected into Mei’s spinal cord. She soon developed a fever and kidney failure and died within days. A year later, Qiu’s team published its preclinical findings in Nature, which Chinese media hailed as “a world-class breakthrough.” Mei’s death and her family’s financial support were not mentioned.

Deaths in clinical trials are not unusual. What is shocking are the regulatory lapses revealed by an investigation published this July in Science and subsequently corroborated by a separate investigation conducted by the Shanghai municipal government, which released its findings last week. The treatment’s consent form, for instance, didn’t warn of the possibility of death. The hospital had approved treatment before toxicology findings showing liver and kidney damage in monkeys that received similar treatments. And, among other crucial omissions, the researchers failed to disclose Mei’s death.

Apparently, this was not an isolated incident. Several researchers told me that Chinese hospitals commonly fail to disclose adverse events. On Aug. 5, STAT reported another death in a gene-editing trial led by Shanghai-based HuidaGene, an incident that had remained undisclosed for about 15 months. (The Chinese team published their findings , including the fatal case, in Cell on Oct. 26.) A founder of a rare-disease organization in China told me, on condition of anonymity for fear of political repercussions, that she had encountered other trials for genetic disorders in which deaths had gone unreported. Recent revelations of undisclosed deaths in clinical trials conducted in China have prompted warnings against the use of Chinese data in U.S. drug development.

As someone who has reported on China’s ethical governance for two decades, this all feels like déjà vu. Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies — that have earned the country a reputation as biotechnology’s “Wild East.”

Back in 2006, patients flocked to China to receive unproven stem-cell therapies . When immunotherapies came into vogue a decade later, bogus advertisements for unproven interventions proliferated online until the health ministry stepped in after the high-profile death of 21-year-old student Wei Zexi. Two years later, biophysicist He Jiankui shocked the world by announcing the birth of the first genetically modified babies created using CRISPR technology.

The response in China to Mei’s death has been divided. Some netizens portray Qiu as a reckless scientist willing to gamble with patients’ lives. Others, including longtime acquaintances, describe him as a diligent scientist committed to helping patients. In some respects, Qiu represents the antithesis of He. After the CRISPR-babies scandal, Qiu openly condemned He’s reckless behavior — only to become embroiled in a comparable scandal himself six years later.

It might be tempting to blame such scandals on individual failings. The deeper questions are: What systemic factors shaped their behavior? What does the incident reveal about China’s Achilles heel in biotechnology—and about the broader culture of international science in which it is embedded? And what can the lessons teach clinical research worldwide?

Fatal Flaw

It would be unfair to suggest that China hasn’t tried to strengthen its ethical governance. The CRISPR-babies scandal prompted deep soul-searching among Chinese scholars and government officials. Since then, President Xi Jinping reportedly championed an “ethics first” approach, contrasting the “science first” mindset often seen in Chinese research. New measures have included incorporating ethics provisions in China’s first Civil Law Code, creating a national ethics committee , and enacting new ethics-review guidelines for clinical research.

But powerful forces are also pushing in the opposite direction. In 2016, China launched Healthy China 2030, making rapid application of emerging medical technologies in clinical practice a priority — not only to address unmet medical needs but to boost national competitiveness. Reforms created a new pathway to translate basic research into clinical applications for cutting-edge technologies overseen by the health ministry, alongside the conventional drug-approval route regulated by the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), China’s equivalent of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). This became widely known as the dual-track regulatory system.

“Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies.”

Under the technology track, clinical trials are often initiated by university researchers working with hospital clinicians rather than companies. Such investigator-initiated trials (IITs) exist worldwide. Until new regulations took effect this May, Chinese IITs were distinctive in that they could proceed with hospital approvals without the national regulatory oversight required for conventional drug trials. Compared with the NMPA route, the faster pathway allowed researchers to assess promising technologies in humans more quickly and at lower costs and help attract investment.

The result was a boom in IITs. By one estimate , more than 40,000 had been registered by April 2026, involving hundreds of thousands of participants and accounting for much of China’s translational research aimed at applying basic research to clinical practice.

China’s IIT model attracted worldwide attention. Kiran Musunuru, an expert on gene therapy at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, told me that “there is a widespread perception” that Chinese-style IITs offer a way to conduct first-in-human trials quickly and inexpensively. U.S. companies are increasingly interested in conducting IITs in China. Some U.S. researchers have even argued that the U.S should adopt elements of China’s model to accelerate drug discovery and enhance its competitiveness.

Critics, however, point to a fatal flaw: quality control. Driven by the pursuit of high-impact papers— whether for career advancement or hospital rankings — researchers rushed into first-in-human trials of emerging technologies. Hospitals are overwhelmed by proposals involving technologies with varying levels of risk. Researchers told me that as many as two dozen applications can be assessed in a single afternoon. In many cases, the process has become “a rubber-stamping exercise,” explained Zhu Wei, a bioethicist at the Shanghai Clinical Research Center.

A recent analysis of Chinese stem-cell IITs found that although a small fraction helped accelerate the application of basic research to clinical practice, most were repetitive, lacked innovation and wasted resources. Musunuru — who led the landmark development of a personalized gene-editing trial for Baby KJ, an infant with a rare life-threatening deficiency of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 that can cause dangerous ammonia buildup in the blood — warns that allowing individual hospitals to approve first-in-human trials of emerging technologies is particularly dangerous, because few researchers have sufficient experience to assess their risks. They would be “operating blind,” he told me, leaving the outcome dependent on “their appetite for risk.” That appetite can be amplified by institutional conflicts of interest. Successful trials of emerging technologies can bring researchers and hospitals fame, career advancement, high rankings and resources. Jing-Bao Nie, a bioethicist at the University of Otago in Dunedin, New Zealand, told me that these incentives can undermine institutional judgment and jeopardize patient safety. In Mei’s case, he noted, the lure of a “world-class breakthrough” may have overwhelmed necessary caution. Political interference, which is common in China, is another way the appetite for risk may outweigh caution. Chinese researchers told me that senior hospital leaders often chair the committees that review trial applications. When they seek to push through major projects led by prominent scientists, other committee members may feel unable to object. Read Noema in print. A central regulator is more insulated from such pressures and can also draw on a far broader pool of expertise. As Musumuru notes, the FDA has an army of experienced reviewers who have assessed successful and failed trials, as well as those involving serious adverse effects. Its decisions are therefore informed by “the widest possible body of knowledge,” he told me. “That’s very reassuring.” Oversight Deficiencies Zhai Xiaomei, a bioethicist at the Peking Union Medical College and a member of the national science and technology ethics committee, was not wrong when she told New Beijing News that the problems exposed by Mei’s tragedy had improved since China’s State Council Order No. 818, which established a new regulatory framework for clinical research and commercial application of cutting-edge biomedical technologies, took effect this May. Under the new rules, only top-tier hospitals can undertake IITs. Trials involving emerging technologies like gene and cell therapy, brain-machine interfaces, transplantation and microbial therapies must undergo further review by the health ministry after hospital approval. Adverse effects must be reported within five working days. Violations can result in fines, suspension or permanent ban on clinical research, loss of licenses and even criminal charges. The scientific community in China and abroad welcomes the new rules. But a researcher working closely with the ministry, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to potential career repercussions, told me that it lacks sufficient staff with the necessary technical expertise to review the large volume of applications. Consequently, the researcher added, the reviews rely heavily on experts from universities and hospitals, with only a handful assessing each case. By contrast, Musunuru told me that the U.S. FDA employs numerous in-house reviewers, many with decades of experience, and dozens pore over each submission. If translating emerging technologies into clinical practice remains a national priority, he argues, China must make sustained investments in regulatory expertise to ensure trial safety and quality. “If translating emerging technologies into clinical practice remains a national priority, China must make sustained investments in regulatory expertise to ensure trial safety and quality.” More troublingly, Order 818 lacks mechanisms to monitor what happens locally and identify violations. It includes neither an inspection process — a crucial component of regulatory oversight in countries such as the U.S. and UK — nor a whistleblowing platform for reporting adverse effects and deaths. Such mechanisms are particularly important in countries where transparency is limited, and the press is not free. Without them, violations may go unnoticed and the penalties risk becoming little more than empty threats. Researchers, like bioethicist Ma Yonghui of Xiamen University, also worry that regulatory exemptions could create loopholes. Military hospitals, for instance, fall outside health ministry rules. The two dozen or so free trade zones across China, particularly in Bo’ao on the tropical island of Hainan, may enjoy special regulatory treatment, potentially attracting foreign researchers and companies seeking to conduct ethically contentious trials they could not undertake in their own countries. There are ample precedents of scientists exploiting countries with weak ethics governance as sites for risky research. In October 2018, one month before the CRISPR-babies scandal, He and John Zhang, founder and medical director of the New Hope Fertility Center in New York City, met Hainan’s vice governor to discuss establishing a clinic in Bo’ao to offer experimental procedures, including heritable genome editing. Zhang had already attracted international attention in 2016 for helping produce in Mexico the world’s first “three-parent baby” to prevent the transmission of mitochondrial DNA mutations from the mother. The procedure involved replacing faulty mitochondria with healthy ones from a female donor during in vitro fertilization, a procedure that was — and still is — illegal in the U.S. Hype & Hope While Mei’s death has prompted renewed soul-searching over China’s ethical failings, it would be a mistake to see it simply as a scientific scandal that can be fixed with new regulations, Nie told me. The case offers a window into people’s relationship with biotechnology in China as well as their hopes and expectations — shaped not only by scientists but by society at large. Over the past decade, rare-disease advocacy organizations have grown rapidly in China, helping improve patient care, pressing for government support and driving research through collecting genetic data, studying disease progression and funding clinical trials. Su Yeyang, an independent anthropologist in Langfang in Hebei province who works with rare-disease communities, told me this has given families a sense of agency. With limited social support and a market-driven drug-discovery model that has failed rare-disease communities worldwide, they are doing whatever they can “to help themselves, their children and their community,” she said. With gene therapy, the “magic cure” long hoped for by many rare-disease patients seems within reach. In one high-profile case, a fledgling company approached Xu Wei, a high-school graduate in his 30s in Kunming, in China’s southern province of Yunnan, to develop a gene therapy for his son. The boy had Menkes syndrome, a rare genetic disorder that impairs copper absorption and causes developmental delays and premature death. The company, with no track record in neurodevelopmental diseases, claimed to have developed the treatment in less than a year. In 2022, the 3-year-old received it at a private hospital in a trial that, based on publicly available accounts, appeared not to include biomarker or behavioral assessments of efficacy. Chinese media reported enthusiastically on anecdotal claims of improvements while downplaying the risks of undertaking such experimental therapies. A patient advocacy leader told me such cases are not uncommon in China, where at least 20 million people are living with rare diseases. They offer hope, whether grounded in evidence or not, and can encourage others to follow. “We try to explain to families that pouring millions into a trial is no guarantee of success” and could even backfire, she says. Even well-educated parents, like Mei’s, may underestimate the complexity of clinical research and overestimate what experimental therapies can achieve. It’s unclear whether Qiu, who was fired by the university last week and barred from participating in scientific research for five years following the government investigation , helped foster such expectations. He has not publicly given his account. But his book, “ The Autism Enlightenment ,” published this April, was revealing. It recounted how, in 2010, he told the mother of a child with Rett syndrome — a rare, genetic neurodevelopmental disorder leading to severe cognitive and physical impairments — that a cure would likely emerge in three to five years. It did not discuss fatal risks often associated with first-in-human trials. It did not mention Jessie Gelsinger, who had a mild form of ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, a condition that can lead to abnormally high levels of ammonia in the blood and died in 1999 from a preventable complication of an experimental gene therapy. “While Mei’s death has prompted renewed soul-searching over China’s ethical failings, it would be a mistake to see it simply as a scientific scandal that can be fixed with new regulations.” Gelsinger was the first person publicly identified as having died in a gene therapy clinical trial, which undermined public trust in the field and set back its progress for decades. Nor did the book draw caution from the death in 2024 of a girl with Rett syndrome in the first brain-directed gene therapy for the condition. In both cases, scientists used the same type of virus as Qiu did. In a society where disability and genetic disease remain stigmatized, and families receive limited support, Mei’s parents placed their hopes in Qiu and gene editing. Like the couple who turned to He Jiankui to protect their children from HIV and the associated discrimination by editing their embryos, they sought a technological solution to social problems. As the Illness Challenge Foundation, a Beijing-based rare-disease advocacy organization, put it after Mei’s death , “responsible innovation should not entice patients to stake their lives in the name of hope.” China’s Gelsinger Moment? Gelsinger’s death in 1999 was a game changer. It’s widely regarded as a cautionary tale of how a toxic combination of scientific hype and insufficient safeguards can jeopardize patient safety. It triggered institutional reforms and significant changes in research culture in the U.S. that were aimed at rebuilding public and regulatory trust. Mei’s death could be China’s Gelsinger moment. It has exposed regulatory failings, a scientific ethos that encourages hype and recklessness, and deeper societal problems surrounding disability and genetic disease. None is unique to China, but they are particularly acute in a country facing a distinctive combination of political and developmental challenges. At the heart of the incident lies the “moral arbitrage” of experimental therapies, a recurrent theme in biotechnological innovation worldwide. On one hand, patients want access to cutting-edge, unproven treatments when they see them as their only hope. On the other hand, such treatments carry risks, which often accompany medical breakthroughs. Navigating the contours between hope and risk requires more than scientific evidence and regulatory rules, Su told me. It demands critical reflection on the culture of international science that places a premium on competition, sensational research, and being first at any cost. It also calls for broader societal dialogues about the diverse notions of human flourishing, the stigmatization of disabilities, and the need for greater support for people living with rare diseases. If China can learn from the failures and undertake the regulatory, scientific and social reforms needed to address its biotech governance failures — and if the rest of the world can look beyond the country’s small number of success stories out of a hidden ocean of low-quality and potentially harmful clinical trials — Mei’s death will not have been in vain. stories.title: Ex-council leader jailed for fraud and tax evasion
stories.summary: Jason Zadrozny sobs in the dock as he is sentenced to 27 months in prison.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Jason Zadrozny was found guilty of nine counts of fraud and four counts of tax evasion in September

Published 27 November 2026

A former council leader accused of inventing a fake heritage society to scam a local authority out of thousands of pounds has been jailed for 27 months.

Jason Zadrozny set up the Ashfield Heritage Society before applying for council funding, which he then transferred into his personal account.

He claimed the cash was "to support heritage projects", but pocketed the money for himself. He was convicted of fraud and tax evasion on 21 September following a trial.

At Northampton Crown Court on Friday, the 46-year-old, of Stanton Hill, sobbed in the dock as Judge David Herbert KC told him he had "failed the electorate and harmed public confidence in the district council by your fraudulent conduct".

The six-week trial heard Ashfield District Council leader and county councillor Zadrozny - of the Ashfield Independents - set up the heritage society in 2018 before applying for funding from Nottinghamshire County Council.

This, the trial heard, included £7,500, requested three days after setting up a bank account for the society, which Zadrozny claimed was "to support heritage projects in Ashfield".

The council issued the funds and they were sent directly to Zadrozny, who deposited them in the account, before withdrawing them in cash in March.

Prosecutors alleged part of the money was used to buy a house with friends.

Jurors were also told Zadrozny was a landlord who did not pay tax on income from four of his properties, estimated in court to be "less than £15,000".

Zadrozny told the jury he did not keep the money for himself, and gave cash from the heritage society to Tony Brewer, a former Ashfield District Council chairman who died from Covid in 2020, to repair war memorials.

At sentencing, Zadrozny was told the total value of his fraud was more than £6,000

Zadrozny also helped set up a Classic Cinema Club for people who liked the Carry On films, which the court heard "was probably legitimate when he set it up" - although he later helped himself to its funds.

The court heard £5,000 was withdrawn in cash from the Ashfield Heritage Society account, while £1,200 was withdrawn from the cinema club.

Zadrozny denied the offences and told the trial the funds he had received were spent on the community.

The former council leader was found not guilty of three counts of fraud.

'A shameful day'

In mitigation, defence barrister Sam Robinson KC said up until 2015, Zadrozny was "a model citizen, in the way he has behaved in his public life but also in his personal life".

Robinson added: "He went off the rails from 2015 onwards. He blew his life spectacularly up.

"It's so easy to look at someone who has unravelled and think why on earth did he do any of this? That's the enigma we're dealing with."

He also said medical experts suggested mental health conditions could have caused "compromised judgement", and "can produce avoidance, indecision and impulsive behaviour".

However, in his sentencing remarks, the judge said Zadrozny had undertaken "dishonest conduct that took place over a number of years".

"I know that today is a shameful day for you," he said.

"When it became apparent that your offending would be uncovered, you sought to cover your tracks in an elaborate series of lies."

The judge said the sentence reflected the "gross abuse of trust", and how the "offending was conducted over a sustained period of time".

Zadrozny resigned as the leader of Ashfield District Council a day after he was convicted

On 12 November, the district council confirmed that Zadrozny resigned as councillor for Larwood, adding there would be no by-election until the local elections in May.

The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) also decided to launch a rapid review of the local authority after MPs raised concerns about a decision to appoint Zadrozny to the council's planning committee in the wake of his conviction.

Ten councillors quit the Ashfield Independents as a result, with some forming a new group called the District Alliance.

An MHCLG spokesperson added: "We have powers to investigate and intervene where councils fail to meet their Best Value Duty, and we're conducting a best-value assessment on Ashfield District Council to ensure it's delivering for local people."

In a letter to Labour MP Michelle Welsh, local government minister Jim McMahon confirmed he had ordered a "rapid best-value assessment" to be carried out into the authority.

Following the sentencing, Theresa Hodgkinson, chief executive at Ashfield District Council said Zadrozny "no longer has an affiliation with the council".

"We do understand why recent events may have damaged confidence in the council and caused concern across our communities," she said.

"Residents are right to expect the highest standards from those elected to represent them, and from their council, and while recent events cannot be changed, we are focused on rebuilding confidence in our council and maintaining and enhancing services and investment into the district.

"Our residents should be reassured that our focus remains firmly on providing high-quality services, investing in our communities and achieving the best outcomes for local people."

stories.title: Government to limit costly legal claims aimed at silencing whistleblowers
stories.summary: An MP cited former Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed as someone who used legal action to suppress his "appalling abuse".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
MPs heard former Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed used legal action to suppress his "appalling abuse"

Published 27 November 2026

The government has pledged to change the law to stop abuse victims, whistleblowers and journalists being silenced by spurious legal actions or threats.

Strategic litigation against public participation, known as Slapps, are often brought by wealthy individuals or companies to stifle scrutiny and suppress matters of public interest.

Existing protections only apply to Slapps linked to economic crime, but the government is now supporting a bill tabled by Conservative MP Sir John Whittingdale to extend protections to all forms of public interest reporting.

Labour's Courts Minister Sarah Sackman said the "justice system should never be a weapon of intimidation".

Speaking in the House of Commons, Sackman said: "The government, working with [Sir John], is determined to stop the wealthy, the powerful using the threat of costly legal proceedings to silence people.

"We are pleased to support the bill and to help ensure that those who expose wrongdoing hold the powerful to account and those who speak out in the public interest are protected."

Opening the debate on his bill, Sir John cited ex-Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed as someone who used legal action to suppress his "appalling abuse of young female employees".

The MP for Maldon said: "That resulted in 27 years in which the information was never publicised."

Hundreds of women have accused Al Fayed of rape, sexual assault and trafficking, after a BBC documentary first publicly detailed the allegations in 2024.

Conservative MP Alicia Kearns said Al Fayed, who died in 2023 aged 94, "turned a culture of abuse and silence into the norm" for women working at Harrods.

The luxury store has previously said it "apologises unreservedly for the sexual abuse inflicted upon survivors by Fayed", and set up a compensation scheme for his victims.

Another example raised by Sir John was journalist Catherine Belton, the author of Putin's People, who faced five legal claims brought by Russian oligarchs and firms.

Sir John also referenced Eliot Higgins, the founder of investigative website Bellingcat, telling MPs he was sued by Yevgeny Prigozhin in 2021 for his tweets suggesting the Russian mercenary leader was associated with the Wagner Group.

He said: "Prigozhin was already sanctioned in this country because of his association yet nevertheless that case was allowed to proceed."

Measures in Sir John's bill include allowing judges to dismiss abusive claims before they go to trial and to protect defendants from exorbitant legal costs.

The UK Anti-Slaap Coalition said last week it "strongly" supports the bill making progress in Parliament although it voiced concerns over its current wording.

It noted there is an "almost impossibly high threshold" to make use of the early dismissal mechanism and offered to work with Sir John and others to refine the bill.

The National Union of Journalists voiced similar concerns, adding the protections must be "truly accessible and robust".

Sir John acknowledged there are concerns over "hurdles" in the proposed legislation which "could act as a deterrent", adding he expects further talks with the minister.

The Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No.2) Bill was debated in the House of Commons on Friday and was given an unopposed second reading, which means MPs endorsed the main principles of it.

It will undergo further scrutiny in the Commons at a later date. It will need to be approved by MPs and peers in the House of Lords to become law.

Reform politician seeks legal action over Senedd ban

Published 8 hours ago

A Reform UK politician banned from speaking in the Senedd after referring to the "replacement" of white people in the UK says he will seek legal action to overturn the decision.

Joe Martin said elected representatives should be able to "speak up for the people who elected them" and raise "difficult subjects".

Reform ended a two-week boycott of most Senedd proceedings on Tuesday in response to the ban, and failed in a bid to remove the parliament's presiding officer .

The Free Speech Union (FSU) campaign group said Huw Irranca-Davies' ruling breached European law, and has sent a pre-action letter challenging it.

The Senedd Commission, which runs the parliament, declined to comment.

On Thursday night, Martin, who represents the Caerdydd Penarth constituency, called the ruling an "unprecedented attack on free speech".

Martin accused what he called a "uniparty" in Cardiff Bay of trying to silence Reform and protect a "cosy consensus".

"That is why I have taken legal action to defend the right to free speech in Wales," he said.

"Every elected representative should have the right to speak up for the people who elected them, without being silenced simply for raising difficult subjects."

FSU said it had sent a pre-action letter to the Senedd Commission, calling for the decision to be reversed, and said it argued that Irranca-Davies "misused his powers".

It also said the decision to prevent Martin from speaking and an order for him to apologise breached Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights , external , which is the right to freedom of expression.

Joe Martin says he is the victim of an "unprecedented attack on free speech"

The ban was handed to Martin earlier this month , after he had asked a minister for a "statement from your government on the demographic replacement of white British people taking place" in the UK.

"Mass immigration and differing birth rates mean that, in just 37 years' time, in 2063, we will be a minority in our own country," he said.

Irranca-Davies had described Martin's words as "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive", but stressed that members could "raise legitimate policy matters" on immigration.

Martin's focus "on race and ethnicity was clearly discriminatory, offensive and detracted from the dignity of the Senedd", Irranca-Davies previously said.

He said Martin would not be called to speak in the Senedd chamber until he had received "clear indication that the member understands the boundaries of acceptable parliamentary conduct and apologises".

Huw Irranca-Davies has warned that without rules eventually it is only the loudest voices that are heard

In June, Plaid Cymru had accused Martin of dangerous rhetoric for claiming attacks from Sudanese asylum seekers were inevitable.

The next day Senedd members walked out during a speech where Martin joked that Welsh students were unable to read and Indian nurses were taking Welsh jobs .

He was later accused by the presiding officer of making offensive remarks in a debate about the Welsh Gender Service .
