stories.title: 'We have no interest in hearing from Huw Edwards', Downing Street says
stories.summary: There has been a backlash against new interviews with the disgraced former BBC News presenter.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 9 hours ago

The prime minister's spokesperson has said broadcasters must "act responsibly" and that "we have no interest in hearing" what Huw Edwards has to say, following a backlash against new interviews with the disgraced former BBC News presenter.

Edwards, who was convicted in 2024 for making indecent images of children, has been interviewed for a Channel 4 documentary plus a podcast by the Observer and Tortoise Media.

"Our thoughts first and foremost will be with the victims of child sexual abuse and exploitation. We have no interest in hearing what he has to say," a Downing Street spokesperson said.

"There are extremely serious crimes and anyone convicted of them must face the consequences of their actions."

The No 10 spokesperson added that broadcasters "are expected to act responsibly and have appropriate regards to their audiences when making decisions".

Pressed on whether the prime minister believed Channel 4 had not acted responsibly, they said: "Channel 4 is editorially independent and decisions about individual programmes and contributors are a matter for them."

During the court case, Edwards admitted three counts of making indecent images of children. That involved having 41 images and videos, which were sent to him on WhatsApp – including some showing a victim aged between seven and nine.

Earlier, Environment Minister Emma Hardy said the plan by Channel 4 made her feel "sick", telling LBC , external it was giving a platform to "someone who is on the Sex Offenders Register".

"That platform doesn't exist for his child victims, does it?... It's not something I could support, and it's definitely not something I'd be watching."

Channel 4 has defended the programme, telling the BBC a "highly experienced director", Patrick Forbes, held Edwards to account with "no questions off limits, revealing his account of what led to his offending and very public downfall".

'Properly challenge'

Conservative MP Dame Caroline Dinenage, chair of the House of Commons culture and media select committee, said the media outlets should "not just act as a platform" for Edwards to have a voice.

Any programme featuring him "needs to properly challenge his past actions" she said, along with raising "still unanswered questions" about whether Edwards will return more than £200,000 he was paid by the BBC , after he was first arrested.

The documentary and podcast will both be released on Tuesday, with some material expected to be published by the Observer on Sunday.

The interviews have also been criticised by three people who previously spoke to BBC News about allegations of Edwards' inappropriate behaviour.

One, who accused him in 2023 of sending them threatening messages, said it was "incredibly bizarre that anyone, big names like Channel Four, are platforming him when he's a convicted sex offender".

The person, who is anonymous and not connected to the criminal case, told BBC News on Thursday Edwards was "clearly trying to do a bit of damage repair" and they were "annoyed that he's being able to air these opinions".

Another person, who said Edwards sent them suggestive and "pushy" messages when they were working at the BBC, and was also not involved in the court case, said: "I'm pretty disgusted they are giving him the air time."

Additionally, a former junior BBC employee, who previously told BBC Newsnight's Victoria Derbyshire they had received inappropriate messages from Edwards, said "it seems a strange and irresponsible decision to give a platform to tell his story after the crimes he has been found guilty of.

"I hope that consideration has been given to his victims."

'A reckoning moment'

Duncan Craig, head of We Are Survivors, which supports male survivors of sexual abuse and rape, said it felt like the media companies were "not thinking about the victims in this particular case".

And it is the wrong time to release these programmes, coming during "a reckoning moment" for abuse in the media, he added.

"[It is] in fact giving somebody a platform that, in some way, shape or form, gives them the ability to nail themselves to the cross. That is not OK."

He added he does "fundamentally believe in rehabilitation" but that "this doesn't feel like it."

In a promotional clip released by the Observer, interviewer Ceri Thomas is seen saying he was "just deeply curious about how it was that a man of such prominence had got himself into this unbelievable, terrible fix".

Craig criticised that choice of words.

"An 'unbelievable terrible fix' isn't somebody sat actively downloading 41 images of child sexual abuse, of which a number of them were at grade A level of of boys aged seven to nine being sexually abused," he said.

BBC broadcaster Nicky Campbell added , external his voice, saying: "I'm rather more concerned for the children in the photographs. What of their lives?"

The Observer, which is owned by Tortoise Media, has been asked for a response to the criticism.

Published 27 November 2026

Four council seats in the West Midlands have been defended by Reform UK after by-elections triggered by the resignation of a councillor featured in an ITV News undercover investigation , external .

Alan Feeney, who later stepped down from the party , was filmed calling Asian homeowners "parasites", in the run up to council elections in May.

In October, he resigned from every post he held on Solihull Metropolitan Borough Council and Birmingham City Council, adding his remarks "were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable".

On Thursday night, Reform held one seat in Shard End on Birmingham City Council and three seats in Castle Bromwich on Solihull Metropolitan Borough Council.

Sarah Myers was voted in to replace Feeney in Shard End, edging Labour by 104 votes, with Birmingham City Council recording a voter turnout of 19%.

Speaking after her win, she said: "I am delighted to have been elected for Shard End, and I'm excited to get to work delivering for local residents.

"Shard End was a former Labour stronghold, and has been badly let down over decades of neglect.

"I look forward to proving that the confidence residents have in Reform is well placed."

'Patriotic party of good'

A Reform UK Birmingham spokesperson said the results showed the public were "sticking with Reform".

"The good people of Shard End recognise that Reform is a patriotic party of good, hard-working individuals who want to fix our country," they added.

The result means that out of 101 councillors on the city council, Reform has 22, while the Green Party has 19, the Conservatives have 16, Labour has 14, and the Liberal Democrats has 12.

Better Birmingham also has seven councillors, Birmingham Independent Workers' Group has five, there are four independent councillors, and two from the Birmingham Independents Group.

Despite Reform having more councillors, Liberal Democrat Roger Harmer remains city council leader , with his party forming a minority administration with the Greens and the Better Birmingham Group.

stories.title: Chris Mason: Immigration stats are down but will that be the end of the issue?
stories.summary: Net migration falling to the tens of thousands is a landmark moment in our collective national conversation about immigration, says Chris Mason.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 27 November 2026

Net migration falling to the tens of thousands is a landmark moment in our collective national conversation about immigration over the last couple of decades.

There is a simple reason for this. We have had years and years strewn with the litter of politicians promising to cut net migration to under 100,000 annually.

But it never happened, until now.

In the latter decades of the last century, net migration was broadly net zero. Sometimes more folk left than arrived. But, around the time that I first arrived as a reporter in Westminster in 2004, the story was changing and would change rapidly.

I have followed every twist, turn, argument and campaign since, both from Parliament and from Brussels.

On 1 May 2004, the European Union expanded hugely, from 15 to 25 members, the biggest expansion in its history.

The bloc's population grew by 74 million people overnight as countries including Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia and what was then the Czech Republic signed up.

And remember, a core plank of EU membership is freedom of movement: the right to travel, live and work anywhere in the club.

Transitional controls on workers from these former communist states could be applied at the time, but the then-Labour government led by Tony Blair chose not to.

The consequences of that decision were as substantial as they were consequential.

Ministers had predicted a minimal impact. But net migration cranked up.

Crucially, this began to ground arguments about sovereignty in the swirling debates about the UK's membership of the EU.

At the time I was a Europe correspondent based in Brussels and a frequent visitor to the European Parliament in Strasbourg.

The UK Independence Party, led by Nigel Farage, were on the rise. But Eurosceptics would tell me privately that their deeply held concerns about the loss of sovereignty, of power, to EU institutions had been a hard sell to many back home. It was an argument, regardless of its merits or otherwise, that felt theoretical and intellectual to many, rather than practical and grounded in day-to-day concerns.

But that changed for many given the scale of immigration people could see.

Plenty of places, particularly beyond the big cities, felt the rapidity of change. Immigration took on a greater political salience.

Should all control over migration be re-imported to Westminster? Such was the growing strength of feeling among many, a sequence of prime ministers began promising to reduce net migration to the tens of thousands.

David Cameron made the promise. The Conservative election manifesto in 2010 harked back to those numbers before the turn of the century. "We will take steps to take net migration back to the levels of the 1990s – tens of thousands a year, not hundreds of thousands."

Five years later, Cameron renewed the promise, in the Conservative manifesto of 2015. The party would "keep our ambition of delivering annual net migration in the tens of thousands, not the hundreds of thousands," it read.

By 2017, Theresa May was prime minister and while the UK had voted for Brexit, it hadn't happened yet. In the Conservative manifesto that year, she promised "controlled, sustainable migration, with net migration down to the tens of thousands."

At the 2019 general election, Boris Johnson was in Downing Street. He didn't repeat the tens of thousands promise, post Brexit, instead arguing for an "Australian-style points-based immigration system" and, crucially, that "overall numbers will come down."

They didn't. Instead, they soared by almost a million – a giant spike on the graph of recent net migration, branded by his critics as the "Boriswave."

Johnson argued that Brexit would mean Westminster would take back control of migration, as leaving the European Union would mean the end of freedom of movement among the member states.

And yes, Brexit did repatriate that power. But this delivered choices, not a guaranteed outcome that the numbers would fall. And Johnson's choices led instead to a spectacular rise.

It took Rishi Sunak's government and the then-Home Secretary Sir James Cleverly to substantially change the rules and so limit the number of visas granted. The incoming Labour government in 2024 inherited these rules and added further to them.

The question now, with the net migration number now in the tens of thousands, is whether immigration will now shrivel as a topic of widespread worry.

How migration feels can be influenced by world view and wealth, politics and geography. Let's take just one aspect of it: the number of asylum seekers being housed in Scotland has increased by 20% over the past year, despite a fall in numbers across the UK as a whole. Glasgow remains the council area with the largest number of people in asylum accommodation in the UK, and there have been increases in areas from Aberdeen to North Lanarkshire which buck the UK-wide trend.

And a lower net figure also does not necessarily mean that the scale of immigration and emigration are low. Large but similar numbers merely serve to almost cancel each other out, numerically. The underlying official statistics set out that an estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June, while 661,000 emigrated.

But just as previous political choices still have consequences now, a persistently low net migration number, depending on who is coming and going, could have consequences in the future. Take Andy Burnham's desire to shake up social care in England, a sector traditionally reliant on arrivals from overseas for much of its workforce. How might it cope? It's one of many potential questions for the future.

For now, as we examine this latest set of statistics, many will reflect that we have collectively as a country – if not everyone individually - exuded an anguish, sometimes an anger at the scale of immigration. It has been one of the standout demographic, social and so political issues of recent times. Perhaps now that conversation turns to a new chapter.

stories.title: Reform UK pledges to scrap hospital parking fees in England
stories.summary: The party says it would compensate NHS trusts for lost fees by charging foreign nationals more for care.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 27 November 2026

Reform UK is promising to scrap parking fees at NHS hospitals in England for all patients, visitors, and staff if it wins power at the next election.

The party said rising parking charges in recent years were unfair, with some hospitals charging up to £20 a day for parking spots.

It says it would compensate hospital trusts for the £300m they currently get from fees each year by raising more from foreign visitors using the NHS.

The health department said it expected charges to be reasonable, with fees used to maintain facilities or put towards funding health services.

Reform's announcement is part of a broader effort by the party to win credibility on the NHS, as it prepares to appoint someone who has worked in the NHS as its health spokesperson in the coming weeks.

Leader Nigel Farage's previous support for an insurance-based healthcare model has harmed the party's standing on the health service, insiders admit.

The latest policy is also part of a series designed to improve the party's recent struggles in the polls by addressing what Reform see as their perceived weaknesses, on Russia, on defence and now the NHS.

Reform's Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick told the BBC the party's spending plans would be set closer to an election, but the party would ensure there would always be "real-terms increases" in funding for the NHS.

Echoing a line traditionally used by British politicians to claim stewardship of the health service, he said: "What we are saying is that the NHS is safe in our hands".

Parking rules

Parking at hospitals in Wales and Scotland is largely free, but NHS trusts in England are allowed to charge and set their own fees and rules.

Government guidance means parking is free for disabled people holding Blue Badges, frequent outpatients, parents of sick children staying overnight and NHS staff working night shifts.

But most visitors are generally expected to pay, along with staff working day shifts.

Reform says its policy to compensate NHS trusts would cost £285m a year to deliver, assuming a £25m annual saving from payment collection costs that would not longer be required.

It plans to recoup lost revenue by charging overseas visitors 200% of the national tariff for NHS services, instead of 150% currently, and extending charges to A&E visits, ambulance services and GP care.

It also says it would make all foreign visitors from countries that do not have reciprocal healthcare arrangements with the UK take out travel insurance covering NHS care, allowing it to "more aggressively collect" money due.

Private contractors

Siva Anandaciva, policy director at the King's Fund health think tank, said parking fees could be a "burden" for those visiting hospitals, but questioned whether Reform's proposals would raise enough to fully compensate trusts.

He said the additional charges on visitors for care would bring extra administration costs, whilst hospitals would need to spend money on systems to ensure free spaces were available to those who need them most.

The experience in Scotland had shown it can also take an "awfully long time" for hospitals to exit contracts with private firms running car pars, he said.

He added: "You might not end up saving as much money as you think".

The health department said it expected fees charged by trusts to be "reasonable and in line with the local area".

"Where charges do apply, the money made is used to maintain facilities, with surplus income put back into the NHS to benefit both staff and patients," a spokesperson added.

In response to parliamentary questions earlier this year, the department also argued , external fees were a "significant control mechanism" to manage capacity given the limited number of car parking spaces available.

stories.body:
At this pivotal moment in American history, let us move forward together to take on and defeat a powerful, greedy and corrupt ruling class

W e are at a pivotal moment in history. Never before in human history have so few people held so much wealth and so much power. And never before have we seen such an unprecedented level of greed, arrogance and irresponsibility on the part of the world’s ruling class.

Here is the good news: leaders from around the world are finally starting to wake up. This week, elected officials and economists from around the world – including four Nobel prize winners – came together in Paris for a “Summit Against International Oligarchy”. As the summit’s proclamation stated, “The explosion of extreme wealth is the major social fact of our time … We are sounding the alarm: billionaires are a threat to our democracies.”

They are right. And that is exactly why I organized, along with other progressives, the Fight Oligarchy tour last year which brought out more than 340,000 Americans in 27 states.

As members of the summit point out, in 1987 the wealth of the richest 0.0001% amounted to the equivalent of 3% of global gross domestic product (GDP). Since then, these 3,000 households have seen their fortunes grow to 17% of global GDP.

At this moment, we live in a world where the top 1% owns more wealth than the bottom 95% of humanity and the gap between the very rich and the poor is growing wider and wider.

Think about it. After all of the wars and revolutions over the last 250 years, after all of the carefully drafted constitutions and hard-fought elections, after all of the wonderful speeches that politicians around the world have given, the top 1% owns more wealth than the bottom 95% of humanity.

In country after country, we are seeing unprecedented income and wealth inequality.

We see it in America today, where the top 1% now owns more wealth than the bottom 93% and one man, Elon Musk, owns more wealth than the bottom 53% of American households.

We see it in Russia, where the latest figures indicate that the wealthiest 500 people in that country control more wealth than the bottom 99.8% of their people.

We see it in France, where more than one out of five children live in poverty, while 53 billionaires own more wealth than the bottom half of the population.

We see it in Africa, where in recent years, nearly 850 million people have struggled with food insecurity, while just four men own more wealth than the bottom 50% of the people on that continent. Yes. Four men own more wealth than half a continent.

We see it in Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar, where a handful of families have unbelievable wealth and power while most of the work done in those countries is performed by impoverished and powerless migrant laborers.

But it’s not just massive income and wealth inequality. It is oligarchs’ control over the global economy. It is oligarchs’ control over much of the media and what people see, hear and read. It is oligarchs avoiding taxes by stashing trillions of dollars in offshore tax havens around the world while the children in their native countries go hungry.

And what are the political implications when the very rich get much richer while working people struggle and feel more and more powerless?

The answer is clear. If people no longer believe that their government is responding to their needs, many of them will give up on democracy and move towards authoritarianism.

And it’s not just Trumpism in the United States. It’s the growth of extreme rightwing parties in Germany, France, the UK and elsewhere.

All over the world, people are asking a very simple question: why should I continue to vote for the same old, same old political parties when my job has been shipped overseas, my factory has been automated, my credit card interest rate is now 25%, I’m unable to retire with dignity, and my children will likely have a lower standard of living than I do – all while the top 1% have never, ever had it so good?

As the country the most billionaires, with a record 989, including 15 of the top 20, the US has a major role to play.

Bottom line: if we are going to improve the lives of working people and protect democracy, the new Democratic majority can no longer continue the failed status quo policies that have devastated so many of our people throughout our country.

This election was about change, real change, and that’s what Democrats must deliver. Now is the time to take on Big Money and fight for an economy that works for all, not just a few.

Yes. We need a wealth tax on billionaires to substantially reduce child poverty, build affordable housing, protect our seniors and invest in the needs of working families.

Yes. We need to guarantee healthcare as a human right by passing Medicare for All.

Yes. We must raise the minimum wage to a living wage – at least $20 an hour – and make it easier for workers to join unions by passing the Pro Act.

Yes. We must strengthen public education and make higher education available to all, regardless of income.

Yes. We must make sure that AI and robotics benefit working families and not just enrich a handful of big tech oligarchs.

Yes. We must ensure that everyone in America can retire with dignity by expanding social security, scrapping the cap on taxable income and restoring traditional defined benefit pension plans.

The new Democratic majority in Congress must act boldly and with an unprecedented sense of urgency. The crises facing our country and the world are much too dangerous to be ignored, or to be dealt with through tepid half-measures.

At this pivotal moment in American history, let us move forward together to take on and defeat a powerful, greedy and corrupt ruling class.

Bernie Sanders is a US senator, and ranking member of the health, education, labor and pensions committee. He represents the state of Vermont and is the longest-serving independent in the history of Congress

stories.title: UK to pay 'participation' fee to deliver EU deals
stories.summary: Details of the contribution towards EU running costs have been revealed in new legal documents.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The UK has agreed the deals in a bid to cut red tape for British companies

Published 26 November 2026

The UK will pay a "participation fee" to the EU as part of the deals agreed by Andy Burnham, according to legal documents.

The surcharge will go towards the running costs of EU agencies and systems required to deliver two of the agreements unveiled by the prime minister last week.

It will be paid in addition to a contribution towards costs that broadly mirrors how EU members contribute to the bloc's shared budget, the documents show.

The government has sought to contrast the financial costs of the deals against their overall effect on the economy, which it estimates will receive an eventual boost by billions a year due to increased trade.

The government is yet to publish an estimate of overall additional costs, but officials said they expected them to be in the low tens of millions per year and "massively outweighed" by predicted economic gains.

British ministers had already said they were prepared to pay towards administrative costs required to implement deals to re-link the UK to the EU's carbon trading regime, and align Britain with the EU's food standards.

Now, details of how the payments will be calculated have been revealed in treaties to deliver the two agreements, which are meant to take effect during 2028.

Legal text for a third agreement agreed last week, on youth visas for 18 to 31 year olds, is expected to be published in the coming days.

Fee details

According to the treaties, the payments will be made as a share of the running costs of three EU agencies, as well as various systems that will be used to implement the food standards and emissions deals.

The bulk of the payments, to be made in euros, will come in the form of an "operational contribution" in proportion to the size of the British economy compared to that of the EU.

This broadly mirrors the way in which EU member states split the cost of their main contributions towards the bloc's overall budget.

But in addition, the UK will also pay a "participation fee" set at 4% of its main contribution figure.

The government has pointed to the 2021 Brexit trade agreement negotiated by the Conservatives, which also applied an additional surcharge to UK contributions towards the cost of relevant EU programmes.

However, any additional contributions are likely to be seized upon by opponents of the latest deals.

Ministers had declined to enter into specifics of the fees during negotiations on the treaties. On Sunday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the latest deals agreed by Burnham were "not about cost to the taxpayer".

'Extraordinary powers'

It comes as the government published separate legislation granting it broad powers to incorporate new EU laws required to implement the agreements, without having to hold a full vote each time.

The food standards deal in particular will mean Britain will have to align with scores of current EU food-related laws that have been updated since Brexit, along with future rules in these areas.

The government argues the new powers are required because it would be impractical to run a full parliamentary process each time UK legislation needs to be updated to make the agreement work.

But it has prompted criticism from opposition parties, because the UK no longer has voting rights at the EU to shape European legislation.

The government argues the UK will get a say on new rules, with the treaty texts confirming British experts can be consulted when new EU laws are being drawn up, with the UK granted "observer" status in certain meetings.

But Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham was showing "disdain for the democratic process" by asking for a "blank cheque to install and enact EU law".

"The prime minister is telling MPs to hand him extraordinary powers whilst having no idea what the EU will actually agree to," she added.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has argued the Burnham's deals would take Britain back into "much of the European Union's single market".

He added: "European economies are not growing as fast as ours. The idea that getting closer to the EU will mean growth for us is a myth."

stories.title: Burnham says UK net migration now under 'sufficient' control
stories.summary: It comes after annual net migration fell to 77,000 - the lowest level this century, excluding the coronavirus pandemic.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 26 November 2026

Andy Burnham said he believes there is now a "sufficient degree of control" of net migration in the UK after it fell to 77,000 in the year to the end of June.

The prime minister said the country is "getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see" but added that there was more work to do.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said it is the lowest recorded net migration estimate since 1997, excluding the coronavirus pandemic.

The Conservatives said the fall was "mainly a result of changes" they made in government, while Reform UK said the figures were "no cause for celebration".

UK net migration at lowest level since 1997 as asylum claims also fall Published 1 day ago

Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats Published 1 day ago

What are the planned changes to immigration rules? Published 3 November

Net migration is a measure of how many extra people are added to the population in a given year.

An estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated, according to the ONS.

In the previous 12 months, UK net migration was recorded as 204,000. It peaked at 944,000 in the year to March 2023.

The 77,000 net migration figure released on Thursday comes more than 16 years after former Conservative leader David Cameron pledged to cut it to below 100,000 before he came to power in 2010.

Speaking to broadcasters, Burnham said: "These figures begin to answer what the public has been saying, we want to see much greater control over the system.

"I'm not going to say all of the work is done and I don't want to appear complacent, but I think we're finally, as a country, getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see."

It was put to Burnham that some people may argue this was a "benefit of Brexit", in light of his desire to explore closer ties with the European Union .

Asked if freedom of movement should be up for discussion as part of the UK's future relationship with the EU, Burnham said in his reply: "I don't think you can say that Brexit did anything other than weaken control of immigration in this country."

The ONS said net migration had "fallen to levels not typically seen since the 1990s".

The biggest factors in Thursday's record low were falls in the arrivals of people coming from outside Europe in three major categories of migration: The number of people coming to the UK to work fell by 45,000, asylum claims fell by 19,000 and the total number of students fell by 33,000.

A fall had been expected because of the tightening of visas rules that began under the previous Conservative government which was then continued by Labour from July 2024.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp argued the Conservatives should receive credit for the decrease in net migration.

He added: "We now need to go even further with an annual legally binding inward migration cap, set by Parliament, at far lower levels.

"British and European people are leaving in their droves because of Labour's high taxes whilst non-EU immigration remains far too high."

Liberal Democrat asylum and immigration spokesman Paul Kohler said Britain faces "serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services".

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage welcomed the drop in numbers, but said he was concerned about "a lot of high skilled big tax paying people" leaving the UK and being replaced by people "who are paying far less in tax".

Meanwhile, his party's Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick said the fall "came about solely because I went to see Rishi Sunak" in 2023 whilst an immigration minister in the Conservative former prime minister's government.

Jenrick, who defected to Reform earlier this year, told the BBC: "I threatened to resign unless he made a series of changes. He did".

"And as a result of those changes to the immigration system, we've got where we are today".

But he added that the changes "didn't go as far as I wanted to," adding this had been behind his resignation from the Tory government a few days later.

A Green Party spokesperson said: "Creating a harsh environment for migrants and asylum seekers is not a measure of success."

Ministerial aides are among nearly 100 Labour MPs who have signed a letter to the prime minister to express their opposition to the Rosebank oil field.

The government could also face resignations from junior ranks if the project goes ahead, the BBC has been told.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is due to make a decision on whether to give the go-ahead for drilling in the oil field off the north-west coast of Shetland within weeks.

The government has remained tight-lipped - both publicly and privately - about what it is likely to do.

Those close to the energy secretary insist that she has not yet made her decision.

But 92 Labour MPs have signed a letter, sent to the prime minister today, urging him not to allow the project to go ahead. Ministerial aides - the most junior rank of government - are among the signatures.

The MP who organised the letter, Catherine Fookes, said: "If Rosebank is approved, champagne corks will pop in the offices of oil companies - but it will not make an iota of difference to my constituents' energy bills.

"The oil belongs to private companies, and will only be shipped overseas to the highest bidder.

"What it will do, however, is accelerate the climate crisis, which is already pushing up food bills, causing devastating winter floods like those we saw in Monmouthshire last year, and fuelling wildfires across our green landscapes in summer."

It's the most visible demonstration yet of the deep divides in the Labour Party over the issue.

The decision about whether to approve Rosebank involves a legal process which technically lies solely with the energy secretary.

Fahnbulleh has, in the past, been regarded as someone personally opposed to the oil field.

Others in the cabinet, including Chancellor John Healey, have let it be known that they would like to see the project given the go-ahead; while the prime minister has repeatedly said he wants to take a "pragmatic" approach to North Sea oil and gas.

But Fahnbulleh insisted last month that she alone would make the final decision and claimed the courts would ultimately side with her if colleagues attempted to overrule her.

Influential pro-Rosebank voices suggested that senior ministers had toned down vocal support as the decision draws closer.

They suggested this wasn't a sign that Rosebank would be vetoed, but because any obvious attempts to pressure the energy secretary might mean her final decision would be subject to a legal challenge.

Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander (left) and Chancellor John Healey (right) accompany Miatta Fahnbulleh on a visit to a Shell gas terminal

A number of MPs say they have heard conflicting claims - with both outcomes being predicted.

What is clearer is that the government's decision will be controversial, whichever way it goes. There is a private and public battle playing out.

Backers of the scheme argue approving it would provide an economic boost. The Conservatives also say it would enhance energy security.

But oil is traded internationally – and the energy secretary has said approving the scheme will not help with immediate cost of living pressures. Rosebank would also be more polluting than Jackdaw, a gas field, which was approved last month.

A fortnight ago, backers of the field were confident it would be approved.

They believed the chancellor's language on energy bills at the Budget , coupled with the lack of political jeopardy that materialised from the approval of the Jackdaw gas field, had made their case stronger.

The same group of MPs believe it would be difficult to reject Rosebank around the same time the prime minister is set to deliver a 10-year plan focused on reindustrialisation.

The government has said oil and gas would be part of the energy mix for many years to come and sources in the trade union movement have suggested that if Rosebank doesn't go ahead, existing inward investment in the North Sea would be put at risk.

While Labour's manifesto upon entering power in 2024 pledged not to "issue new licences to explore new fields", it does pledge to honour existing ones.

In 2023, the then Conservative UK government granted a licence for Rosebank and a legal challenge followed.

The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that the government had made the approval unlawfully, leaving the current Labour government to make a new decision on whether to give the go-ahead.

The mood among some pro-Rosebank MPs changed this week, with several who back approval telling the BBC they were now worried it would be blocked.

The BBC has spoken privately to Labour MPs involved in the debate, before the letter was sent to the prime minister, to get a sense of how divisive it is proving.

One ministerial aide said: "There are quite a few of us who are considering our positions. I'm in that group. We want to see leadership on climate change."

Another aide who said they might quit added: "There a group of us for whom we became Labour MPs because of climate change. It is the issue that motivated us into politics."

Other aides – known in Westminster as parliamentary private secretaries – told the BBC they were opposed, but would stay in their jobs if it went ahead.

Another said they thought there were increasing signs the prime minister would not be able to carry his party with him if the scheme was given the thumbs up.

And another said the energy secretary might have to resign if it goes ahead, given her scepticism about the project.

It has been reported in recent weeks that members of her team are encouraging opponents to make their feelings known. The BBC has been told the same.

One MP, who backs Rosebank, said the behind-the-scenes operation had been so effective, the scheme was up in the air again.

That has led to some anger at the energy secretary.

One minister says: "Miatta has boxed herself in with how she's handled Rosebank. It's outrageous if she's encouraging MPs to speak up over Rosebank. We should get on and do it."

Like the decision itself, the exact timeframe is unclear. But some opposition figures expect it mid-December.

Whatever happens, it will be controversial and has already exposed splits in the Labour Party.

stories.title: Mandelson kept shares as ambassador despite conflict of interest fears, documents show
stories.summary: The peer was sacked as ambassador last year over his relationship with the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 26 November 2026

Lord Mandelson still held shares in his lobbying company eight months after becoming US ambassador, despite government concens about conflicts of interest, newly released documents show.

The peer was sacked as ambassador last year by Sir Keir Starmer following revelations about the extent of his relationship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

This 85-page release is the third since MPs voted to publish documents aiming to reveal behind-the scenes-discussions about how he was appointed to the role.

The documents were previously withheld due to the Metropolitan Police investigation into allegations Lord Mandelson had passed market-sensitive government information to Epstein.

Sir Olly Robbins was sacked as head of the Foreign Office by Sir Keir Starmer during the scandal when it emerged Lord Mandelson had been granted clearance for the role despite concerns being raised by vetting officials.

The newly released documents highlight that Lord Mandelson was able to keep his shares in Global Counsel, the lobbying company he co-founded, while serving as ambassador to Washington.

They reveal civil servants' concerns about the risk of perceived conflict of interest.

But selling the shares was clearly not a condition of him taking up the role.

Part of that is because of the desire in Sir Keir's government at the time to have Lord Mandelson in Washington as quickly as possible.

That is exemplified in an email from Sir Olly, saying a process to police Mandelson's conflicts of interest could be "up and running in a light touch way".

Another factor is selling shares in a private company like Global Counsel, which advised high-profile clients including Chinese-owned TikTok, US tech firm Palantir and pharmaceutical firm GSK. requires finding a new buyer or selling them back to the company.

But the documents also reveal Lord Mandelson had not sold his shares back to Global Counsel because their offer was not the "fair value". Another attempt to sell to a different buyer fell through.

The result was Mandelson kept his shares, and while in office tried to set up a meeting between Global Counsel and a key Donald Trump advisor, as well as taking the firm's advice on a speech on Britain's role in the world.

Lord Mandelson remained a shareholder until February 2026 , the same month the company went into administration.

Sir Olly wrote to David Lammy in August to tell him Lord Mandelson still had not divested himself of his Global Counsel shares

Emails about his dealings with his Washington counterparts show a close relationship, with one message from an unnamed White House official in April 2025 telling Lord Mandelson his label as the "Prince of Darkness" could not be "farther from the truth".

Ahead of a speech he was due to give on Britain's role "in the age of Trump", documents show him seeking advice from a Global Counsel employee in August 2025, during his time as ambassador.

The exchange contains feedback from an unnamed Global Counsel director, who suggested he should use "warmer language" about China and tone down "parts of your apologia of the Trump administration".

The director warned: "Scepticism of [the Trump administration] is now so deep – at least in the public policy-interested world outside government – that it would be counterproductive/unpersuasive if you came across as having drunk the Kool Aid."

Lord Mandelson responds to say he would water down his language, and in another email tries to arrange an "under the radar" lunch meeting to discuss China and trade between a GC employee and someone from the US President's Council of Economic Advisers.

On the domestic front, Lord Mandelson also sent texts to Sir Keir's then chief of staff Morgan McSweeney in September 2025 offering advice on a cabinet reshuffle.

He suggested moving Darren Jones to lead the science and technology department as a way to "solve your Darren issue", although McSweeney did not respond until after the reshuffle decisions had been made, with Jones given a newly-created role as chief secretary to the prime minister.

Lord Mandelson has yet to comment on the most recent release of papers relating to his appointment.

He has repeatedly let it be known he believes he has not acted criminally, did not act for personal gain and is cooperating with the police.

No charges have been made. A Met Police spokesperson told the BBC: "Our investigation into alleged misconduct in public office is ongoing."

Speaking to journalists in the Downing Street garden following the release of the documents, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would address culture change for Westminster as part of his 10 year plan, which he said will be published next month.

He said: "I've come back in as something of an outsider into the system and I see a lot of things that I think need to change to improve the political culture of this country and to strengthen the public interests when it comes to all of these issues."

Security minister Dan Jarvis told MPs: "The government recognises that action needs to be taken in response to the issues raised by Mandelson's appointment."

He said action had already been taken to strengthen the vetting and appointments process, including strengthening the management of conflicts of interest.

Future appointments will not be made before security clearance has been granted, he said, adding that review by Sir Adrian Fulford of vetting procedures was nearing completion.

A separate review by Sir Anthony Finkelstein into use of personal messaging services including WhatsApp and Signal for business purposes is expected to be published in January next year.

stories.title: Burnham joined by former PMs at Widdecombe service
stories.summary: Hundreds of guests attended including Andy Burnham, David Cameron, Liz Truss and Boris Johnson.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham and a number of previous prime ministers attended the service

Published 26 November 2026

Andy Burnham was joined by former prime ministers as he attended a memorial service for the late politician Ann Widdecombe.

Hundreds gathered for the Service of Remembrance at Westminster Cathedral on Thursday afternoon, including David Cameron, Liz Truss, Boris Johnson and Rishi Sunak.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage and deputy leader Richard Tice, along with former Conservative Chancellor Philip Hammond and Speaker of the House of Commons Sir Lindsay Hoyle, were also in attendance.

Bishop James Curry, the Auxiliary Bishop of Westminster, led the service after the Archbishop of Westminster, Richard Moth, was taken to hospital earlier.

Reform UK's chairman Lee Anderson, deputy leader Richard Tice and leader Nigel Farage were among those at the service

Moth, who is the head of the Catholic Church in England and Wales, underwent tests after he "felt unwell", Westminster Diocese said.

During the memorial, tributes were paid by Widdecombe's nephew, Reverend Roger Widdecombe, and independent crossbencher Lord Alton of Liverpool.

Widdecombe's nephew said his aunt's death was "a tragedy," but added the service was to "pay tribute to Aunt Ann" and "celebrate and thank God for a life well lived".

He said: "Words such as integrity, brave, kind, delightful, indefatigable, interested, tireless, fun, all express something of the amazing woman that Ann was."

He noted his aunt was "certainly a lot of fun," recalling family anecdotes which prompted guests to laugh.

Finishing the eulogy, he said: "We loved her very much, and we'll miss her."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham shakes hands with former prime minister Rishi Sunak at the service

The service, which lasted about 70 minutes, featured a motet, a psalm and two hymns sung by the Westminster Cathedral choir.

The prime minister was later seen leaving the cathedral with former prime ministers Rishi Sunak and Boris Johnson.

Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform UK's justice spokeswoman, was found dead at her home in Haytor, on Dartmoor, Devon, on 9 July, aged 78.

Politicians past and present gathered for the service remembering Ann Widdecombe

Joshua Kerry, 28, of Byrley Road, Rotherham, South Yorkshire, was charged with her murder.

A trial before a High Court judge is scheduled for 8 June, and a plea and case management hearing on 29 January.

Widdecombe's family announced plans for a public memorial service following her death.

The late politician served as Conservative MP for Maidstone and the Weald in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.

Former Conservative leader Sir Iain Duncan Smith attended the service

She became a member of Reform in 2019 as a party spokeswoman.

Away from politics, she appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing in 2010 and was a runner-up on Celebrity Big Brother eight years later.

In the 1990s she converted to Catholicism, a move she later described as the best decision she ever made.

stories.title: New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause
stories.summary: Text of the treaties was published this afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 26 November 2026

The government and the EU have published the texts of two treaties agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.

The treaties were published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.

The deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay "reasonable and proportionate costs" to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal.

Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would scrap the deal while Reform UK's Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay.

The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the future of the UK-EU relationship.

The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

Two of the three legal texts were released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.

A new assessment of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country was also released.

EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme Published 2 days ago

Badenoch challenges Burnham over university fees for EU students Published 2 days ago

Farage helps launch new campaign against the UK rejoining the EU Published 2 days ago

Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost the export of major agricultural commodities.

The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements."

"It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."

A plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.

The treaty text also contains finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules. The UK will be invited to attend European Commission meetings and expert groups as an observer, as well as taking part in emergency food security planning.

However, the UK will not be given voting rights.

Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, are detailed in the legislation.

Such powers will enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny.

Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week , the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".

Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.

Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.

Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

stories.title: UK net migration at lowest level since 1997 as asylum claims also fall
stories.summary: Net migration figures of 77,000 in the year to the end of June mark the lowest this century outside of the Covid pandemic.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 26 November 2026

Net migration to the UK has fallen to 77,000 in the year to the end of June - the lowest level this century, other than during the pandemic, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures show.

Excluding the limited movements of people during the worldwide travel restrictions in 2020, the figures show the number of people arriving in the UK, minus those leaving, tumbled 92% from the record high of 944,000 in the year to March 2023.

The ONS said this was the lowest net migration since 1997.

Net migration is a measure of how many extra people are added to the population in a given year.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures showed there was now "a sufficient degree of control" over the migration system.

Three charts that show how migration surged and then fell Published 1 day ago

Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats Published 1 day ago

German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds Published 1 day ago

What are the planned changes to immigration rules? Published 3 November

The prime minister went on to say: "I'm not going to say all of the work is done, and I don't want to appear complacent, but I think we're finally as a country getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see."

The underlying official statistics show that an estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the figures showed that Labour had "delivered" after Conservative failures - but Chris Philp, her Tory shadow, said restrictions introduced by his party before the 2024 General Election were behind the falls.

The 77,000 figure is also the first time the UK has seen net migration in the tens of thousands since former PM David Cameron's controversial pledge 16 years ago to reach such a level.

The biggest factors in Thursday's record low were falls in the arrivals of people coming from outside Europe in three major categories of migration: The number of people coming to the UK to work fell by 45,000, asylum claims fell by 19,000 and the total number of students fell by 33,000.

These number had been expected to fall because of the tightening of visas rules that began under the previous Conservative government which was then continued by Labour from July 2024.

The effect of those policies, plus emigration from the UK, has meant that while net migration had already begun to fall, it more than halved in the last 12 months alone.

Mahmood said the figures showed the government had "restored control".

"We have brought net migration to 77,000, down 92% from its peak under the Conservatives," she said. "Where they failed, we have delivered for the British people."

This is a reference to the so-called "Boriswave" after Brexit. When the UK left the EU and its freedom of movement rules, Boris Johnson's government allowed in many more people to work and study from other parts of the world.

That led to the record-breaking arrivals in the year to March 2023. Johnson's successor, Rishi Sunak, introduced major restrictions on visas in the last months of his government.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the falls were a result of those changes.

In a post on X, he called for an "annual legally binding inward migration cap, set by Parliament, at far lower levels".

Dr Ben Brindle of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, an impartial expert body, said: "We are entering an unusual period where immigration has come down and may still have further to fall - but we still have relatively high emigration, at least for the time being.

"Most of those emigrants are non-citizens, including people who arrived a few years ago when immigration was very high. That could push the net migration figures down even further next year, but the downwards blip is unlikely to last forever."

In the year to June some 73,000 people arriving in the UK seeking asylum - down from 93,000 the previous year.

As of September, the number of people who were waiting for a decision was 41,000, down 49% on the previous year.

The Home Office said that these changes were driven by speeding up the system in taking decisions and a fall in the arrivals of new claimants via "illegal entry routes" - largely meaning English Channel small boats.

As a result, the number of people accommodated in September by the Home Office was 93,000 - 16% lower than the year before. Some 52 hotels that had been dedicated to asylum seekers have been emptied this year. While some 140 are still in use the total number of people in hotels has fallen 64% to 13,000.

Responding to the latest statistics, Reform UK's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said the figures were "no cause for celebration".

"This population explosion is why British people struggle to get a GP appointment, can't get housing and our prisons are overwhelmed."

Liberal Democrat asylum and immigration spokesperson Paul Kohler said: "Britain faces serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services."

A spokesperson for the Green Party added: "Creating a harsh environment for migrants and people seeking asylum is not a measure of success. The British people are overwhelmingly compassionate and will not be taken in by the dangerous and opportunistic narratives of the far right."

stories.title: UK reservists contacted as 'threat environment' rises, Streeting says
stories.summary: It comes after reports that reservists have received letters telling them to prepare to be called up for war.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Reservist soldiers training at Longmoor camp in southern England in 2024 (file photo)

Published 26 November 2026

The Ministry of Defence has written to ex-military personnel to check their contact details and skills against the backdrop of a rising "threat environment", Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has said.

It comes after The Times and the Telegraph reported that reservists who previously served in the Armed Forces have received letters telling them to prepare to be called up for war.

Streeting told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that this meant should they ever be needed "either for a national disaster here at home or for a more serious threat or conflict elsewhere" then they would "know where our strategic reserve is" and what their skills were.

"I want the country to be alert, not alarmed," he said.

"You can't not look at what's going on in Europe and not be concerned about a threat environment which has deteriorated in recent years and is sadly increasing," Streeting told Today.

"We saw last Friday a very serious incident – the incursion into Polish airspace by Russian missiles, we've seen state-sponsored terrorism waged by Russia across Europe, we've obviously had incidents concerning Iran around RAF bases here in the UK.

"And so against that backdrop, against that threat environment, the government and the country has to be ready to face down those risks."

He added: "Because the more ready we are the less likely we are to find ourselves in a conflict, in a war, that is my goal, that is the goal of this government."

Streeting told BBC Breakfast that "if, God forbid, this country did find itself at war" and there was then an inquiry, the Ministry of Defence would be criticised if the government had not kept its records up-to-date."

The Telegraph reported that the letters offered opportunities to volunteer , external for training and exercises.

This is not a case of pressing the panic button for imminent war, but more one of good housekeeping.

When Britain went to war in Iraq in 2003 the MoD had a poor grasp of who might be available to serve, what current skills they had and what their up-to-date contact details were. So they obviously don't want to be in that situation if there is a national crisis in the future that triggers a mobilisation.

Twenty three years on, the Ukraine war has changed everything. It's brought a hot war to the very borders of Nato, it's exposed the dangers of having too few troops available, but most of all it has changed the nature of warfare.

People who have spent their adult lives never touching a weapon can turn out to be extraordinarily skilled drone operators, those with a talent for electronics, radio and signals work have a vital role to play in electronic warfare.

So this exercise by the government, probably long overdue, is about knowing who can do what and where they can be contacted.

Justin Crump, a former Army officer and now CEO of the business intelligence firm Sibylline, told the BBC: "Ukraine has shown us the importance of mobilising civilian skills and approaches in modern warfare. This is a first step, and an overdue one in many ways, with the effort likely to increase through early 2027. [It is] very much a part of deterrence and not an intention to use people".

He said veterans - a sometimes misleading term for men and women who are often in peak physical shape and fitness - that he has contacted have generally responded positively to the move. "After all", he said, "they signed up to help before, but want to make sure their enhanced skills and talents are valued".

The MoD's decision to contact ex-military personnel comes after news that the UK has signed an £8bn contract to upgrade its nuclear submarine fleet, which the defence secretary said would help get the country "warfighting ready".

Meanwhile, Streeting also praised the Duke of Sussex's "patriotic spirit" after the former Army officer said he would rejoin the armed forces again if needed.

Asked whether there could be a role for Harry, the defence secretary told Today: "I'm always happy to talk to him about how we can work together, whether that's through his Invictus Games, which does a brilliant job supporting our veterans and giving them opportunities to take part in those amazing and inspiring competitive sporting events, but he does have experience to bring to bear."

Streeting praised the "service he's given to our country" and the fact he had spoken about his "willingness and readiness to serve".

"I think that's exactly the sort of patriotic spirit we're looking for," he said.

"I think it's that sort of patriotic spirit we'll find throughout our strategic reserve."

Last week, Harry, who spent a decade in the forces and served on the front line in Afghanistan, said: "If asked to sign up again, if the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country, alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel."

stories.title: Ministers hiding behind data protection on Sir Galahad bombing files, says veteran
stories.summary: Falklands veterans demand UK government release more files from 1982 inquiry.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Forty-eight people were killed when Sir Galahad was attacked in 1982

Published 26 November 2026

A Falklands War veteran who was left severely burned in an attack on his ship has accused ministers of hiding behind data protection in refusing to release all files on the bombing.

The undefended supply ship Sir Galahad was hit by Argentinian planes in June 1982 killing 48 people, including 32 Welsh Guards.

The Welsh Guards had previously been blamed for not leaving the ship earlier, but files released later cleared them of any blame .

Simon Weston said veterans "just want to know who is responsible for making terrible decisions".

The UK government said it had to strike a balance between respecting legal obligations and giving veterans the answers they needed.

A 1982 Royal Navy inquiry was held in private and its findings unreleased.

Excerpts have been released over time, including in 2024, when two files were released.

But five files comprising 308 witness statements are closed and, under the terms of the Public Records Act 1958, are not due to be released until 2065.

More than 100 were injured in the bombing. Another eight died on the Sir Tristram while dozens of others were injured.

Weston, and fellow veteran Mike Hermanis, attended a Commons debate on the management and disclosure of records from the inquiry on Wednesday.

'We're not interested in anything but the truth'

Weston, 65, a former Welsh guardsman, said he was "disappointed" by the response.

He said ministers must "stop hiding behind GDPR", referring to the regulations that have governed data protection since the 2010s.

"It wasn't meant for what went on in '82 and statements that were made in '82. So we feel that people will be hiding behind a law that wasn't theirs to hide behind," he said.

"We're not interested in anything other than the truth. We just want to know who is responsible for making terrible decisions."

The scheduled release date was too late to help anyone, he said.

"We'll all be dead by then and it benefits not us or the families.

"It's been a terrible tortuous 44 years and some of the families have passed away since then, sisters and brothers of the bereaved, and it's just not fair on them."

Simon Weston accuses ministers of hiding behind data protection regulation

Hermanis, 64, from Newport, was on board the ship as a 19-year-old guardsman.

He said ministers' refusal to unseal files until 2065 was "very deflating".

"After being there for 90 minutes and at the 11th hour, that was a sledgehammer blow to us.

"But we've been campaigning for 44 years, so we'll just keep on going, keep knocking, somebody's going to open our door."

He said watching the debate had been "overwhelming" and he was moved to tears by the amount of support from backbench MPs.

"These MPs, they're all different parties, and they came together to give us truth, justice and transparency. That's all we want: honesty."

Transcripts 'missing from the record'

Labour's Newport East MP, Dame Jessica Morden, secured the debate after being contacted about the issue by Hermanis, who is her constituent.

Morden also said ministers had confirmed to her that some of the transcripts and tape recordings of key witnesses given as part of an inquiry into the bombing were "missing from the record, having somehow been lost at an unknown point over the years".

"It is really hard to see, 40 years later, how the current approach can be justified," she told MPs.

The former Conservative leader Iain Duncan Smith, who served in the Scots Guards, said it was "shameful" the Welsh Guards had been blamed when those above them had made mistakes.

Chris Evans, the Labour MP for Caerphilly, said he was "utterly disgusted" the Welsh Guards had been blamed for the tragedy, and said the UK government had a "chance to put that right".

The minister for the armed forces, Louise Sandher-Jones, said she wanted to be clear the Welsh Guards were not at fault.

"The Welsh Guards were absolutely not to blame in any way. In fact, as we have heard, they showed amazing bravery and heroism with their actions that day," she told MPs.

But she said ministers had legal obligations they must respect.

"Section 40 of the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) protects the personal information of living individuals. That is why those files currently should remain closed until 2065. There are also obligations under the Data Protection Act 2018," she told MPs.

Sandher-Jones also said it was important to consider carefully "whether the wider impact of releasing reports to do with a historical event means that, in some future tragedy, we constrain being able to get to the truth".

stories.title: Heathrow third runway plans 'should be grounded'
stories.summary: The runway plans do not fully address issues including climate tests, the Transport Committee says.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
An artist's impression showing three runways at Heathrow Airport

Published 26 November 2026

The government has "failed to make the case" for Heathrow Airport's expansion, the chair of the Transport Committee has said, as a highly anticipated report on the £33bn project is published.

Ruth Cadbury said the draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement did not adequately address noise, air pollution and climate tests.

"Plans for a third runway should be grounded for now and the government should go back to the drawing board," she said.

Downing Street has repeatedly said the prime minister would wait for the Transport Committee's report, among other factors, before deciding whether to back the scheme. The prime minister's office has been contacted for comment.

What's the plan for a third runway at Heathrow Airport? Published 30 January 2025

The report said the climate test was examined in the context of the recent advice from the Climate Change Committee.

The results showed the west London airport's expansion would not be compatible with the UK's carbon budgets or net-zero targets, it said.

The committee said both the air quality test and the noise test should be strengthened, adding that there was a lack of certainty over the cost of expansion that could affect the prices paid by airlines and passengers.

It also raised concerns over a lack of extensive plans to improve public transport, such as new rail lines into Heathrow from the west and south.

"If a third runway is to get off the ground, then government also needs to strengthen the air quality test and noise tests, develop plans for improving public transport and bottom out how much it will cost airlines and passengers to use an expanded Heathrow," Cadbury said.

She also called for "robust analysis" to set out what would happen if decarbonisation goals were missed.

"Expansion should not go ahead at any price, or at any cost to society or the environment," the report said.

'Weight of evidence'

A spokesperson for the Department for Transport said the government had made clear that Heathrow expansion could only go ahead if it met four tests covering economic growth, climate change, noise and air quality.

They added: "We note the findings from the committee's report and will consider these as we continue to review responses to our consultation on the policy framework underpinning expansion."

Ruth Cadbury's west London constituency is close to Heathrow Airport

Paul McGuinness, chair of the No 3rd Runway Coalition group, said the expansion would "leave the country worse off, once the negative costs are taken into account".

However, Heathrow's chief executive Thomas Woldbye said the "overwhelming weight of evidence and support remains strongly behind Heathrow expansion".

"Successive governments, independent commissions and industry experts have repeatedly concluded that you either expand Heathrow so the UK can compete and grow, or you accept a steady erosion of the UK's connectivity and global competitiveness," he said.

Cadbury, Labour MP for Brentford and Isleworth in west London, has been outspoken about her opposition to the expansion .

Lord Khan, who was the MP for Tooting before becoming London mayor in 2016, also opposes a third runway .

He previously told BBC Radio London that noise, air pollution and climate change targets were his main concerns.

Then-chancellor Rachel Reeves announced last year the government was backing the scheme .

She previously said it would add 0.5% to the UK's GDP, although updated government forecasts in June recalibrated this figure at just 0.05%.

'100,000 jobs'

The Transport Committee's report said the government had positioned expansion as "critical" to national growth, but that "the case for this designation applying to Heathrow expansion has not been made".

Heathrow is the UK's busiest airport, serving more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways.

The number of flights, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average - if a third runway is built.

It is estimated the project would create 100,000 jobs.

But it would see homes demolished, rivers diverted and the M25 motorway rerouted through a tunnel between junctions 14 and 15.

The new runway was scheduled to open by 2035, subject to plans being submitted and approved, but Heathrow has since suggested a date of 2039 due to planning and regulatory issues.

stories.body:
Administration is suggesting an added 20% tax on Chinese imports, which would bring the total to about 40%

US politics live – latest updates

Donald Trump is proposing new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the European Union, that would go into effect early next year, the office of the US trade representative said on Wednesday.

The administration is proposing an additional 20% tax on Chinese imports, which would bring the total tax to about 40%. Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.

In February, the supreme court ruled Trump’s so-called Liberation Day tariffs illegal. The court issued a narrow decision saying the administration had improperly used a specific emergency powers law to implement the tariffs, but did not broadly curb the president’s power to introduce new tariffs.

The administration is now using section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 as the legal basis for the new rounds of tariffs. The law gives the executive branch power to respond to unfair foreign trade practices after conducting formal investigations.

Though the White House did not give a timeline for the new tariffs, it said they could go into effect in January at the earliest. The US trade office said it would hold hearings on the new tariffs and its investigation into the unfair trade practices on 25 January.

This is the second major batch of section 301 tariffs, after the White House announced a broad slate of tariffs on more than 80 countries in July, including the UK, Mexico and Canada, saying the countries had failed to enforce bans on forced labor. A lawsuit fighting those tariffs is currently awaiting a decision in the court of international trade.

“For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America’s manufacturing base,” the US trade representative, Jamieson Greer, said in a statement on Wednesday.

“President Trump is proposing to take action to bring about the elimination of these unfair acts, policies, and practices. In doing so, we can level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.”

Tariffs have proven unpopular with US voters, who handed Democrats a decisive victory in the midterm elections that will give the party control of Congress. The Yale Budget Lab estimates that tariffs currently in effect have added an additional $900 annually in costs for each US household.

The rising cost of living was the number one issue for voters ahead of November’s midterm elections, according to a Harris Poll survey for the Guardian. An earlier Harris poll found seven in 10 Americans blamed tariffs for higher prices.

Consumer prices rose an annualized 3.8% in October, the Bureau of Economic Analysis announced on Wednesday, the highest rate since May and well above the Federal Reserve’s 2% annual target.
